What Is Life?
A question with no easy answer

A rock, a flame and a seed all look quiet from far away. Yet only one of them is alive. Biology starts with a simple question: what makes the seed different? There is no single test. Scientists instead list a set of traits that living things share. Knowing the list helps you read every later lesson, from cells to ecosystems.
Seven traits of living things

Most textbooks use a checklist. A living thing: Is made of cells (one or many). Uses energy to run its chemistry. Grows and develops . Reproduces . Responds to its surroundings. Keeps a stable inside (homeostasis). Evolves over generations. Think of it like a shop: it needs stock (matter), power (energy), a counter that reacts to customers, and branches that open over time.
Homeostasis: staying steady

Your body stays near 37 °C whether it is Delhi in June or Shimla in January. This is homeostasis, coined by Walter Cannon in 1926 building on Claude Bernard's idea of a steady inner environment. A sensor notices a change (you get hot). A control centre compares it with a set point. An effector acts (you sweat). The change shrinks and the loop stops. It works like a room thermostat.
Metabolism: life's chemistry

Metabolism is all the chemical reactions in a cell. Some build things (anabolic), like making protein. Some break things down (catabolic), like burning glucose for energy. A fire also uses fuel and gives off heat, but a fire does not regulate itself, grow by its own plan or pass on instructions. Life does all three.
Levels of organisation
Life is built in layers, each with new abilities. A single bacterium is one cell and one organism. You are about 30 trillion cells working together.
Where do cells come from?

In 1665 Robert Hooke saw tiny boxes in cork and called them cells. Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Schwann (animals, 1839) said all living things are made of cells. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow added that every cell comes from a pre-existing cell. Together these form the cell theory .
Borderline cases: viruses

A virus has genes and evolves, but it has no cell and cannot make energy. It reproduces only inside a host cell. Many biologists call it non-living outside a host; others call it a 'life-like' agent. It shows that the line is fuzzy. Think of a virus as a set of instructions with no factory. Outside a host it is just a protein shell around DNA or RNA, as inert as a seed packet in a drawer. Once it docks on a cell, it hijacks the cell's machinery to copy itself. Martinus Beijerinck coined the idea of a 'contagious living fluid' in 1898, and Wendell Stanley crystallised tobacco mosaic virus in 1935, showing it could form crystals like a chemical.
Can life come from non-life?

People once believed maggots arose from rotting meat. In 1668 Francesco Redi covered some jars with gauze and found no maggots on the meat. In 1859 Louis Pasteur used swan-neck flasks: broth stayed clear because germs could not reach it. This ended the idea of spontaneous generation. In 1953 Stanley Miller sparked gases like early Earth's and made amino acids, showing how life's building blocks may have formed.
Common mix-ups

Check yourself Moving does not equal alive. Clouds and rivers move; plants barely do. Growth is not just getting bigger. Crystals grow, but from outside, not by metabolism. A mule is alive even though it cannot reproduce. Traits are judged for the whole group of life, not each individual.
J.C. Bose and the response of plants

Jagadish Chandra Bose (1858-1937) built the crescograph, which magnified plant growth by about ten thousand times or more. He showed that plants respond to touch, heat and chemicals in measurable ways, blurring the line between 'living' responses in plants and animals. He founded the Bose Institute in Kolkata in 1917.
Key takeaways and questions

Life is defined by a checklist: cells, energy, growth, reproduction, response, homeostasis, evolution. Cell theory: all life is cellular and cells come from cells. Redi and Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation. Viruses sit on the edge of the definition. Think about it: Why is fire not alive though it uses fuel and grows? Would you call a virus alive? Defend your view.
The Cell: Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes
A city smaller than a dust grain

Every cell is like a tiny city. It has a wall or border, power plants, factories, a library, a post office and a waste team. Once you know the parts, diseases, antibiotics and even cancer start to make sense. There are two big city plans: the simple one (prokaryote) and the planned, walled-room one (eukaryote).
Two cell types

Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus. DNA floats in a region called the nucleoid. Eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi, protists) keep DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus and have many membrane-bound organelles.
The nucleus: the library

The nucleus holds DNA and is wrapped by a double membrane with pores. Inside, the nucleolus builds ribosome parts. Robert Brown named the nucleus in 1831. Instructions are copied here as messenger RNA and sent out through the pores. Think of the nucleus as a library that never lends out its only copies. Instead, a cell makes a working photocopy, the mRNA, and sends it to the workshop. The nuclear envelope has thousands of nuclear pores that act as guarded doors, letting small molecules pass and checking larger cargo. Inside, DNA is wound around proteins called histones into chromatin , which packs about two metres of DNA into a space a few micrometres wide.
Ribosomes, ER and Golgi: factory and post office

Ribosomes are the protein makers. The rough ER (studded with ribosomes) makes proteins for export; the smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies. The Golgi (found by Camillo Golgi, 1898) sorts and packs them.
Mitochondria and lysosomes

Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP, the energy currency. They have their own DNA and double membrane. Lynn Margulis (1967) argued they were once free bacteria swallowed by a bigger cell: the endosymbiotic theory . Chloroplasts have a similar story. Lysosomes hold enzymes that digest worn-out parts, like the recycling unit.
Plant cell extras

Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall , a large central vacuole for water and storage, and chloroplasts for photosynthesis. Animal cells have centrioles for division and no wall. Each extra has a job. The wall, made of cellulose, works like a brick box that stops the cell bursting when it fills with water, so plants stay upright without a skeleton. The central vacuole can fill up to 90 percent of the cell and presses the contents against the wall, giving firmness (a wilted plant has lost this pressure). Chloroplasts hold chlorophyll and turn sunlight into sugar. Like mitochondria, they carry their own small DNA.
The cytoskeleton

A web of protein fibres gives shape and lets the cell move. Microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules act as scaffolding and rails for transport. Cilia and flagella are built from microtubules. Picture the cytoskeleton as the beams of a building plus its railway. Microtubules are hollow tubes of tubulin and serve as tracks; motor proteins such as kinesin walk along them carrying cargo, like a porter on a rail. Microfilaments of actin are thin and help cells crawl and pinch in two. During division, microtubules form the spindle that pulls chromosomes apart. Unlike a fixed frame, the cytoskeleton is constantly built and rebuilt.
From lenses to electron beams

Hooke used a microscope in 1665. Anton van Leeuwenhoek saw living bacteria in the 1670s. The electron microscope, built by Ernst Ruska in 1931, revealed organelles far too small for light. Albert Claude and later George Palade used spinning (centrifugation) to separate parts and study them.

Red blood cells in humans lose the nucleus, so not every eukaryotic cell has one. Another frequent slip: 'all cells are tiny'. A hen's egg yolk is a single cell, and some nerve cells in a giraffe stretch over a metre. Also, the cell wall belongs to plants, fungi and bacteria, not only plants. Membranes and Transport
The smart border

Every cell is wrapped in a membrane that decides what enters and leaves, like a gate with a guard. If it fails, the cell dies. Salt balance, nerve signals, drug action and even why a pickled mango stays dry all depend on membranes. The membrane is selective: oxygen and small fatty molecules slip through, while ions and large molecules need special doors. Think of a railway station with ticket gates, where only passengers with the right ticket enter. Salting raw mango works because water leaves the fruit cells by osmosis. A membrane is about 7 nanometres thick, thousands of times thinner than a hair.
The fluid mosaic model

In 1972 S.J. Singer and Garth Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model. The membrane is a double layer of phospholipids . Each has a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails. Tails hide inside, heads face water on both sides. Proteins float in it like boats on a sea, and cholesterol adjusts fluidity.
Passive transport: no energy

Molecules move from high to low concentration. This is diffusion . Small non-polar molecules like oxygen slip straight through. Water moves by osmosis , often through channels called aquaporins (Peter Agre, Nobel 2003). Large or charged molecules use facilitated diffusion through channel or carrier proteins.
Active transport: with energy

Moving things uphill, from low to high, needs ATP. The sodium-potassium pump pushes 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP. Jens Skou discovered it (Nobel 1997). It keeps nerve cells ready to fire and drives much of your energy use. Think of it as a pump hauling water uphill: it needs fuel. The pump changes shape after taking a phosphate from ATP , releasing sodium outside, then grabbing potassium and flipping back. Because it keeps more Na+ outside and more K+ inside, the cell stores an electrical charge, like a charged battery. Nerves and muscles use that stored charge to fire signals.
Osmosis in daily life

Water moves toward the saltier side. Put a raisin in water: it swells. Salt on a slug or on pickles pulls water out. Plant cells in fresh water become firm (turgid); in strong salt they shrink (plasmolysis).
Bulk transport

Large particles cross inside bubbles. Endocytosis brings material in (phagocytosis means 'cell eating', pinocytosis 'cell drinking'). Exocytosis sends material out, as when nerve cells release signals. Steps of endocytosis: the membrane dents inward around the particle, pinches off as a bubble called a vesicle , and carries it inside. In exocytosis the reverse happens, and a vesicle fuses with the outer membrane and empties outside, like posting a parcel. White blood cells use phagocytosis to swallow bacteria. Insulin is released from pancreas cells by exocytosis. Both processes need ATP. Remember it as a delivery van: cargo goes in the van, not through the wall.
Early clues

Ernest Overton (1890s) noticed that fat-soluble substances enter cells easily, hinting at a fatty membrane. In 1925 Gorter and Grendel extracted lipids from red blood cells and found enough to cover the cells twice, suggesting a double layer. The Gorter and Grendel result is an old but neat piece of reasoning: if the lipids covered twice the cell surface, the membrane must be two layers thick. Their numbers were a little off, though the conclusion held. In 1935 Danielli and Davson added proteins to the picture, and in 1972 Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model , where proteins float in a sea of lipids.

Oral rehydration therapy

During cholera epidemics, Indian-origin doctors like Dilip Mahalanabis used oral rehydration solution during the 1971 refugee crisis. It works because glucose helps sodium enter gut cells through a carrier, and water follows by osmosis. It has saved millions of children. Mahalanabis worked with refugees near the Bangladesh border, where IV fluid ran short, and he used a salt and glucose drink instead; deaths from cholera fell sharply. The Lancet later called ORS potentially the most important medical advance of the 20th century. A simple home version uses clean water, a pinch of salt and sugar.

Enzymes and Metabolism
Why you can digest a roti

Without help, digesting starch would take years. Your body does it in hours because of enzymes, biological catalysts that speed reactions up millions of times. Lactose intolerance, fever, food spoilage and many medicines all come down to enzymes. An enzyme works like a key made for one lock: it grabs a particular molecule, helps it change, and lets it go unchanged. Salivary amylase begins breaking starch in a roti while you chew, which is why bread tastes slightly sweet if you hold it in your mouth. Enzyme names usually end in -ase, such as lipase for fats and protease for proteins.
What an enzyme is

Nearly all enzymes are proteins (some RNA). An enzyme lowers the activation energy , the push needed to start a reaction, and is not used up. It acts on a substrate at a pocket called the active site . Analogy: a key and lock. Better: a glove that tightens around the hand (induced fit, Daniel Koshland, 1958).
What changes enzyme speed

Temperature: rises with heat until the enzyme folds out of shape (denatures). pH: pepsin works at pH 2, trypsin near 8. Substrate amount: speed rises then levels off when all enzymes are busy (Michaelis and Menten, 1913). Inhibitors: block the active site or bend the enzyme.
Cofactors and vitamins

Many enzymes need helpers. Metal ions like zinc or magnesium are cofactors. Small organic helpers are coenzymes; many are made from vitamins, such as NAD from niacin (B3). That is why vitamin lack causes disease. A coenzyme works like a rechargeable carrier that ferries electrons or small groups between reactions. Humans cannot make many of these helpers and must eat the vitamins. Lack of niacin causes pellagra, and lack of thiamine (B1), a part of a coenzyme for breaking down glucose, causes beriberi, a disease linked in the 1890s to polished rice by Christiaan Eijkman.
Metabolic pathways

Cells link reactions into chains. The product of one enzyme is the substrate of the next. Often the final product switches off the first enzyme, called feedback inhibition , like a tap that closes when the tank is full. A pathway is like an assembly line in a factory, where each worker does one step. Glycolysis is a ten-step pathway that breaks glucose in your cells. Feedback inhibition stops waste: when enough product accumulates, it binds the first enzyme at a site away from the active site (an allosteric site ) and slows it. The cell thus makes only what it needs.
ATP: the energy coin

Cells pay for work using ATP (adenosine triphosphate). Breaking its last phosphate releases usable energy. A person turns over about their body weight of ATP each day, recycling it from ADP. ATP works like a small coin that is spent often and refilled constantly. A cell holds only a few seconds' supply, so it is remade from ADP and phosphate in mitochondria using energy from food. Karl Lohmann discovered ATP in 1929, and Fritz Lipmann showed in 1941 that it is the cell's energy currency. Muscle contraction, nerve pumps and building proteins all spend ATP.

Many doubted him until others confirmed it. Buchner's discovery ended the idea that fermentation needs a 'vital force' inside living cells: the chemistry could happen in a flask. Sumner's urease crystals then proved enzymes are real molecules. John Northrop later crystallised pepsin and trypsin, and the three shared the 1946 Nobel Prize. Today X-ray images show enzyme shapes in detail. Today X-ray crystallography, developed by the Braggs, shows an enzyme's shape atom by atom.

Photosynthesis
The sun, bottled

Almost every meal you eat, and almost all the oxygen you breathe, traces back to photosynthesis. Plants, algae and some bacteria capture sunlight and store it as sugar. It is the entry point of energy into nearly every food chain. The overall change is easy to remember: carbon dioxide and water, with light, become glucose and oxygen. A leaf works like a solar kitchen, and the sugar can be burned right away, turned into starch for storage in a potato, or built into cellulose for new wood. Fossil fuels such as coal are ancient sunlight stored by this process. Joseph Priestley (1771) and Jan Ingenhousz (1779) showed that plants restore air and need light.
The overall equation
6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light gives C6H12O6 (glucose) + 6 O2. It happens in chloroplasts , in two linked stages: light reactions in the thylakoid membranes, and the Calvin cycle in the fluid stroma.
Light reactions

Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light, reflecting green. Light energy excites electrons in photosystem II. Water splits, releasing O2 and replacing electrons. Electrons pass along a chain, pumping protons; this drives ATP synthase. Photosystem I re-energises them to make NADPH. The oxygen you breathe comes from water, not CO2.
The Calvin cycle

Worked out by Melvin Calvin with Benson and Bassham in the 1950s (Nobel 1961). The enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto a five-carbon sugar. Using ATP and NADPH, the product is turned into G3P, a three-carbon sugar. Some G3P leaves to make glucose; the rest rebuilds the starter sugar.
C3, C4 and CAM plants

RuBisCO sometimes grabs oxygen instead of CO2, wasting energy (photorespiration), worse in heat. C4 plants like maize and sugarcane first fix CO2 in a separate cell type, concentrating it. CAM plants like cactus and pineapple open pores at night to save water. Think of C3 as the basic design, used by rice, wheat and most trees. Hot, dry days push the pores ( stomata ) shut to save water, which lets CO2 run low, so RuBisCO wastes more effort on oxygen. C4 plants add a pump that raises CO2 near RuBisCO, like a turbocharger, so maize and sugarcane do well in tropical heat. CAM plants store CO2 overnight as an acid and use it by day behind closed pores.
What limits the rate

Light intensity, CO2 level, temperature and water. F.F. Blackman (1905) proposed the law of limiting factors: the scarcest factor sets the speed. Think of a queue at a railway counter: the slowest step decides how fast people get through. On a dim morning, light is the limit and more CO2 changes nothing. At noon, CO2 or heat may be the limit instead. Above about 40 °C, enzymes begin to lose shape and the rate falls. Farmers use this idea: greenhouses add light and CO2, and irrigation prevents water from becoming the limit.
Where does the oxygen come from?

Jan van Helmont (c.1640s) grew a willow and found most of its mass came from water, not soil. Joseph Priestley (1771) showed plants refresh air; Jan Ingenhousz (1779) showed light is needed. Samuel Ruben and Martin Kamen (1941) used heavy oxygen to prove O2 comes from water.

Cellular Respiration
How food becomes movement

The roti you eat does not directly power your muscles. Cells first burn glucose step by step and capture the energy in ATP. Understanding this explains breathing, why exercise makes you pant, why yeast makes dough rise and how some poisons like cyanide kill so fast.
The overall equation

C6H12O6 + 6 O2 gives 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy (about 30-32 ATP per glucose). It is the reverse bookkeeping of photosynthesis. It runs in four steps and burns glucose slowly, so energy is not wasted as one big flame.
Glycolysis

Glycolysis splits glucose (6 carbons) into two pyruvate (3 carbons). It needs no oxygen, happens in the cytoplasm and nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH. It is probably the oldest pathway, found in nearly all life. Worked out by Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas in the 1930s.
Krebs cycle

Hans Krebs described it in 1937 (Nobel 1953). Acetyl-CoA joins a four-carbon molecule to form citrate, which is stripped of carbons step by step, releasing CO2. Each turn yields NADH, FADH2 and a little ATP. The carbons you breathe out come from here. Think of the cycle as a wheel that turns, takes in two carbons from acetyl-CoA each round, and gives off two carbons as CO2. It runs in the mitochondrial matrix . The wheel's real prize is the carriers NADH and FADH2, like loaded delivery vans that head for the electron chain.
Electron transport chain

NADH and FADH2 hand electrons to protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane. This pumps protons across, building a gradient. Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making most of the ATP (chemiosmosis, Peter Mitchell, 1961). Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and becomes water. Imagine water pumped uphill into a dam, then let down through a turbine. The protons are the water and ATP synthase is the turbine; it even spins as protons pass, as shown by Paul Boyer and John Walker (Nobel 1997). One glucose gives roughly 30 ATP in total. Without oxygen to clear electrons away, the chain jams and ATP production collapses.
Without oxygen: fermentation

When oxygen is short, cells keep glycolysis going by recycling NADH. Muscles make lactic acid. Yeast makes ethanol and CO2, which makes bread rise and brews beer. Fermentation gives only 2 ATP per glucose.

Cell Division: Mitosis and Meiosis
From one cell to you

You began as a single cell. Cell division built you, heals your cuts, and makes eggs and sperm. When its control fails, the result is cancer. Two kinds exist: mitosis (copying) and meiosis (shuffling for reproduction). Count the scale: an adult has about 30 trillion cells, all descended from one fertilised egg by repeated mitosis. Each day you lose and replace billions, such as skin and gut lining cells. Think of mitosis as a photocopier making identical pages, and meiosis as shuffling a deck of cards before dealing a hand. Walther Flemming first described the thread-like chromosomes in dividing cells in 1882.
The cell cycle

A cell spends most time in interphase (G1 growth, S DNA copying, G2 preparation), then divides in M phase. Checkpoints, run by proteins like cyclins, ask: is DNA intact, is the cell ready? Failure of checkpoints (for example p53 mutation) can lead to cancer. Imagine a factory that checks quality at three gates. The G1 checkpoint asks if conditions are good, the G2 checkpoint asks if DNA copying is complete and error-free, and the spindle checkpoint asks if every chromosome is attached before they are pulled apart. The p53 protein, called the 'guardian of the genome', can pause the cycle or trigger cell suicide ( apoptosis ) when damage is too great. Lee Hartwell, Tim Hunt and Paul Nurse found the cycle controls (Nobel 2001).
Mitosis: one cell, two copies
Walther Flemming described it in the 1880s. Result: two identical cells with the same chromosome number (2n to 2n).
Meiosis: halving the number

Meiosis has two rounds of division and makes four cells with half the chromosomes (n). It happens in the ovary and testis. Eggs and sperm are n, so fertilisation restores 2n. Meiosis I: homologous pairs separate. Meiosis II: chromatids separate, like mitosis. Before meiosis I, DNA is copied once, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids. Early in meiosis I, matching chromosomes pair up and swap segments in crossing over , which creates new combinations. Pairs then line up at random, a process called independent assortment . A human has 23 pairs, so there are over 8 million possible combinations of chromosomes in one egg or sperm even before crossing over.
Why meiosis creates variety

Two tricks shuffle genes. Crossing over in prophase I swaps pieces between paired chromosomes. Independent assortment lets each pair sort at random: humans have 23 pairs, so about 8 million combinations before crossing over.
When it goes wrong

Failure of chromosomes to separate (nondisjunction) gives extra or missing chromosomes. Down syndrome is trisomy 21 (Jerome Lejeune, 1959). Cancer arises when a cell ignores stop signals and divides without end. The risk of nondisjunction rises with maternal age because egg cells wait in the ovary for decades paused in meiosis. Extra chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome, first described by John Langdon Down in 1866, with the cause found by Lejeune. Missing or extra sex chromosomes cause conditions such as Turner syndrome (X0). In cancer, mutations in genes for growth signals (oncogenes) or brakes (tumour suppressors) accumulate.
Seeing chromosomes

Flemming stained and watched chromosomes in the 1880s. Theodor Boveri and Walter Sutton (c.1902) linked chromosomes to Mendel's factors. Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan (1956) fixed the human number at 46. Think of Sutton and Boveri as detectives: chromosomes come in pairs and are shared out during meiosis, just as Mendel's factors are, so the two must be linked. Thomas Hunt Morgan proved it with fruit flies around 1910. Before 1956 scientists believed humans had 48 chromosomes; better preparation, using a salt solution that swelled cells so chromosomes spread out, showed 46.

Mendel and the Laws of Inheritance
Why you look like your parents, but not exactly

Children resemble parents yet differ from them. For centuries, people thought traits blended like paint. A monk with a garden proved otherwise, and founded genetics. Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian monk in Brno, grew about 28,000 pea plants between 1856 and 1863 and counted the offspring. He reported in 1866 that traits are carried by separate units (now called genes ) that pass on whole, like beads on a string and not like mixed paint. His work was ignored until 1900, when de Vries, Correns and Tschermak rediscovered it independently. Mendel's pea garden gave the first clear rules, and they still guide breeding of crops and animals today.
Gregor Mendel's pea experiments

Between 1856 and 1863, in Brno, Gregor Mendel crossed pea plants. He picked clear either-or traits: tall or short, round or wrinkled seed, yellow or green. He used pure-breeding lines and counted thousands of plants. He published in 1866; the work was ignored until 1900, when de Vries, Correns and Tschermak rediscovered it.
Law of dominance and segregation

Cross pure tall (TT) with pure short (tt). All offspring (F1) are tall. Dominant allele T hides recessive t. Self the F1 and the short trait returns in about one quarter of F2: ratio 3 tall : 1 short. Law of segregation: each plant carries two alleles for a trait and they separate into different gametes.
Using a Punnett square

For Tt x Tt: gametes T or t from each parent. The four boxes give TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Genotype ratio 1:2:1; phenotype ratio 3:1. A test cross with a tt plant reveals whether a tall plant is TT or Tt. Think of a Punnett square as a chance table, like tossing two coins. Reginald Punnett drew it around 1905. Write one parent's gametes along the top and the other's down the side; each box is one equally likely meeting of an egg and a pollen grain. A test cross is useful because tt can only give t, so any short offspring proves the tall parent carried t. If all offspring are tall, the parent was most likely TT.
Independent assortment

For two traits together (round/wrinkled and yellow/green), the dihybrid cross gives 9:3:3:1 in F2. Genes for different traits sort independently, true when they lie on different chromosomes. Mendel's second law says that the allele a gamete gets for one trait does not affect which it gets for another, like shuffling two separate decks. A plant RrYy can make four gamete types (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in equal numbers, and 16 boxes then give 9 round yellow, 3 round green, 3 wrinkled yellow and 1 wrinkled green. Genes lying close together on the same chromosome break this rule because they travel together (linkage), as Morgan found in 1910s.
Beyond Mendel

Incomplete dominance: red x white snapdragon gives pink. Codominance: human AB blood group shows both A and B. Multiple alleles: ABO has IA, IB and i. Sex-linked traits: colour blindness and haemophilia on the X chromosome (Morgan, fruit flies, 1910). Polygenic traits: height and skin colour involve many genes.
Mendel's luck and care

Mendel chose pea because it has many clear traits, short generation time and controllable crosses. Statistician R.A. Fisher later noted his counts were suspiciously close to expected ratios; the debate continues, but the laws hold. Boveri, Sutton and Morgan tied genes to chromosomes. Peas were a smart choice: they self-pollinate, but Mendel could open a flower and dust it with chosen pollen. He used seven traits, such as seed shape and flower colour, and started with pure-breeding lines. He also counted large numbers, which makes ratios stand out from chance. Fisher's 1936 criticism concerned how neat the numbers were, not the laws themselves, which hold across all sexually reproducing species.
Watch out

Fix these Dominant does not mean common or better; polydactyly is dominant yet rare. A 3:1 ratio is a probability, not a guarantee for four children. Traits do not blend; genes stay intact. Also, a recessive trait does not vanish; it is hidden when a dominant allele is present, and it can reappear in a later generation, just as Mendel saw. Many human traits, such as height and skin colour, depend on many genes and the environment, so simple ratios do not apply. Also, 'recessive' does not mean rare or weak. In many human traits the common version is recessive, and a recessive allele can be carried quietly by millions of people who show no sign of it at all.
Blood groups and inherited disease in India

The ABO and Rh systems matter in transfusion. India has high carrier rates of sickle cell and thalassaemia in some regions, and the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (launched 2023) screens carriers. Recessive disorders are more frequent where cousin marriage is common. Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO groups in 1900 (Nobel 1930), and A and B are codominant over O. Sickle cell and thalassaemia are inherited when both parents pass on a faulty recessive allele, so each child of two carriers has a one in four chance of the disease. Carrier screening and counselling help families plan.
Key takeaways and questions

Dominance, segregation, independent assortment. Monohybrid 3:1 and 1:2:1; dihybrid 9:3:3:1. Real inheritance includes codominance, multiple alleles, sex-linkage, polygenic traits. Think about it: Two tall plants give a short offspring: what are the parents' genotypes? Why can two parents with blood groups A and B have an O child?
DNA: Structure and Replication
The instruction book of life

Every cell in your body holds about two metres of DNA, packed into a nucleus a few micrometres wide. It carries the recipe for you. Forensics, ancestry tests, vaccines and cancer drugs all begin here. Imagine a thread of DNA as long as a thin string: stretched out, the DNA from all your cells would reach to the Sun and back many times. A cell copes by winding DNA around proteins and coiling it tight, like a rope wound into a ball. The four letters A, T, G and C, written in a different order, hold the instructions for every protein. Friedrich Miescher first isolated DNA from pus cells in 1869, and Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed in 1944 that it is the genetic material.
What DNA is made of

DNA is a long chain of nucleotides . Each has a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate and one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), cytosine (C). The order of bases is the code. Analogy: a ladder twisted into a spiral. Sugar-phosphate backbones are the rails; paired bases are the rungs.
Chargaff's rules

Erwin Chargaff (1950) found that in any DNA, A equals T and G equals C in amount. This hinted at pairing: A-T by 2 hydrogen bonds, G-C by 3. Chargaff's numbers made no sense until the structure was solved. Purines (A, G) are double-ringed and pyrimidines (T, C) single-ringed, so a pairing of one big and one small base keeps the width of the ladder constant, like rungs of equal length. This complementary base pairing is why one strand predicts the other: if one reads ATGC, the partner reads TACG. James Watson and Francis Crick used this rule, along with X-ray images from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, to propose the double helix in 1953.
Strands run opposite

The two strands are antiparallel . One runs 5' to 3', the partner 3' to 5'. This matters for how DNA is copied. Picture two lanes of a motorway running in opposite directions. The numbers 5' and 3' refer to carbon atoms on the sugar at each end of a strand. Enzymes can add new bases only to a 3' end, so one new strand (the leading strand ) is made smoothly, while the other (the lagging strand ) is made in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, named for Reiji Okazaki (1968). An enzyme called ligase then joins the pieces.
Replication: copying

Helicase unzips the helix at an origin, forming a fork. Primase lays a short RNA primer. DNA polymerase adds matching bases, only in the 5' to 3' direction. The leading strand is made smoothly; the lagging strand in pieces (Okazaki fragments, 1968). Ligase joins the pieces. It is semi-conservative : each new helix has one old and one new strand. Polymerase also proofreads, with about one error in a billion bases.
Packing two metres into a cell

DNA wraps around proteins called histones , forming beads called nucleosomes. These coil into chromatin and then into chromosomes, visible during division. Humans have 3 billion base pairs per set of chromosomes. Prokaryotes keep a circular chromosome, plus small rings called plasmids that scientists later used as gene carriers.
Discovering the helix

Frederick Griffith (1928) saw bacteria transform. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) showed the transforming substance was DNA. Hershey and Chase (1952) confirmed it with viruses. Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image (Photo 51, 1952) and Maurice Wilkins's data helped Watson and Crick propose the double helix in 1953 (Nobel 1962 to Watson, Crick, Wilkins). Meselson and Stahl (1958) proved semi-conservative copying.
Watch out

Fix these A gene is not the whole DNA; it is a stretch of it. DNA is not the same as a chromosome; chromosomes are DNA wrapped on proteins. Franklin's contribution is often understated. Also, DNA copying is semi-conservative : each new double helix keeps one old strand and one new, as proved by Meselson and Stahl in 1958 using heavy nitrogen. Franklin's Photo 51 gave the key clue of the helix, yet the Nobel Prize of 1962 went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins, and she had died in 1958.
Khorana and DNA fingerprinting

Har Gobind Khorana (born in Raipur, now Pakistan, 1922) chemically synthesised the first artificial gene in 1970 and shared the 1968 Nobel for cracking the genetic code. At CCMB, Hyderabad, Lalji Singh developed DNA fingerprinting in India, used in forensic and paternity cases. The GenomeIndia project has sequenced 10,000 Indian genomes (announced 2025).
Key takeaways and questions

DNA is a double helix of four bases; A-T, G-C. Replication is semi-conservative: helicase, primase, polymerase, ligase. Griffith to Hershey-Chase proved DNA is the genetic material. Think about it: If one strand reads ATGC, what is the other? Why is semi-conservative copying good for accuracy?
From Gene to Protein
Recipe to dish

DNA is a recipe book kept safely in the nucleus. Proteins are the dishes: enzymes, muscle, antibodies, haemoglobin. How a recipe becomes a dish is the central dogma of biology, stated by Francis Crick in 1958: DNA to RNA to protein. The recipe analogy goes further. DNA never leaves the nucleus, just as a rare cookbook stays in the library, so the cell copies one recipe (a gene) as mRNA. The ribosome in the kitchen reads it and assembles the dish from amino acids. There are 20 amino acids, and their order decides how a protein folds and what it does. Haemoglobin has 574 of them in four chains.
The central dogma
Cells copy a gene into a messenger (mRNA), then read the mRNA to build a protein.
RNA vs DNA

RNA has ribose sugar, uses uracil (U) instead of T, and is usually single-stranded. Types: mRNA (message), tRNA (carries amino acids), rRNA (part of ribosomes). Why RNA instead of DNA? Ribose makes RNA less stable and easier to dispose of, which suits a short-lived message, like a sticky note, while DNA is the archive. Uracil replaces thymine, so a DNA stretch TAC is copied as AUG. Some RNAs even act as enzymes, called ribozymes , found by Cech and Altman (Nobel 1989), which supports the idea that RNA came before DNA in early life.
Transcription

RNA polymerase binds a promoter . It reads one DNA strand and builds mRNA. In eukaryotes, the raw copy is edited: a cap and tail are added and introns are cut out, leaving exons (splicing). Think of it as copying a page for the kitchen. RNA polymerase unwinds a short stretch of DNA and slides along the template strand , pairing each base with a matching RNA base (A with U, G with C). It stops at a terminator signal. In humans, the average gene has several introns, and alternative splicing lets one gene produce different proteins by choosing which exons to keep. In bacteria there is no nucleus, so translation can begin while the mRNA is still being made.
The genetic code

Every three bases (a codon ) specify one amino acid. There are 64 codons: 61 code for 20 amino acids, AUG means start (methionine), and UAA, UAG, UGA mean stop. The code is nearly universal and redundant. Nirenberg and Matthaei cracked the first codon (UUU = phenylalanine) in 1961; Khorana made synthetic RNAs to decode the rest.
Translation

Ribosome attaches to mRNA and finds AUG. tRNA with a matching anticodon brings its amino acid. The ribosome links amino acids with peptide bonds and moves on. At a stop codon, the chain is released and folds into a protein. The ribosome is like a reader that moves along a ticker tape three letters at a time. It has two subunits that clamp the mRNA, and sites that hold the tRNA carrying the growing chain. Each tRNA has an anticodon on one end and the matching amino acid on the other, like a taxi labelled with its passenger. Many ribosomes can read one mRNA together, forming a polysome , so many copies are made quickly. Newly made chains then fold, helped by chaperone proteins.
Proof of the code

Beadle and Tatum (1941), working on bread mould, proposed one gene, one enzyme. Brenner, Crick and colleagues (1961) showed the code reads in triplets. Marshall Nirenberg, Khorana and Robert Holley shared the 1968 Nobel. Reverse transcriptase (Temin and Baltimore, 1970) showed RNA can also be copied into DNA, as in HIV.
Watch out

Fix these Codon (on mRNA) and anticodon (on tRNA) are different things. Not all DNA codes for proteins; much is regulatory or non-coding. The code is redundant, not ambiguous: one codon never gives two amino acids. The genetic code was cracked by Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei in 1961, who found UUU codes for phenylalanine. There are 64 codons for 20 amino acids, so several codons give the same amino acid ( degenerate code). Mutations in a third letter often do nothing for that reason. Another point: the code is read in strict groups of three from the start codon, so shifting the starting point changes the entire message. Mutations in the third letter often do nothing. Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei began cracking the code in 1961 by finding that UUU codes for phenylalanine, and 64 codons share 20 amino acids.
Khorana and sickle cell

Khorana's synthetic RNA experiments in the 1960s completed the decoding. In sickle cell disease, one base change (A to T) swaps one amino acid in haemoglobin (glutamic acid to valine), a disease that affects many tribal communities in India. Har Gobind Khorana, born in Raipur (now in Pakistan), built RNA chains with set patterns of bases at the University of Wisconsin, and shared the 1968 Nobel Prize with Nirenberg and Robert Holley. His synthetic repeating sequences confirmed which codons matched which amino acids. The sickle cell change shows how one letter in 3 billion can alter one protein, so haemoglobin clumps when oxygen is low and bends red cells into a sickle shape.
Key takeaways and questions

DNA to mRNA (transcription) to protein (translation). Codons of three bases; AUG starts, three stop codons end. Eukaryotic mRNA is spliced before use. Think about it: Translate DNA TAC into the mRNA codon and anticodon. Why is a near-universal code evidence of common ancestry? Key terms: a gene is a stretch of DNA with the recipe; transcription happens in the nucleus; translation happens on the ribosome in the cytoplasm. A codon has three bases, and the order of codons sets the order of amino acids. Remember that exons are expressed, introns are removed, and a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) codes for no amino acid at all.
Gene Regulation and Epigenetics
Same DNA, different cells

A nerve cell and a liver cell have the same DNA, yet look and work completely differently. The reason is that each cell switches on only the genes it needs. Regulation explains development, cancer and why identical twins drift apart. Your body has around 200 cell types, all with the same roughly 20,000 genes. Think of the genome as a huge library of which each cell borrows only the books it needs: a liver cell reads the books on detoxifying, a nerve cell reads those on signalling. Regulation also acts like a dimmer, not just an on-off switch, setting how much of each protein is made and when. François Jacob and Jacques Monod worked out the first such system in bacteria in 1961.
Genes have switches

Think of a recipe book where each cook opens only some pages. Regulation can act at many points: whether a gene is copied, how the mRNA is edited, how long it lasts and how the protein is used. The most common control is at transcription.
The lac operon

Francois Jacob and Jacques Monod (1961, Nobel 1965) studied how the gut bacterium E. coli handles lactose. An operon is a group of genes under one switch. No lactose: a repressor sits on the operator and blocks the genes. Lactose present: it binds the repressor, which lets go, and enzymes to digest lactose are made.
Switches in complex cells

Eukaryotes use transcription factors , proteins that bind promoters and distant enhancers . Hormones like oestrogen act this way. A master gene, like Hox genes, can set the body plan: wrong switch, extra legs on a fly. Think of an enhancer as a volume knob far from the speaker but linked by a wire: DNA can loop so that a distant enhancer meets the promoter. Transcription factors work in teams, so a few dozen can create thousands of different patterns, like chords on a piano. Hox genes, found by Edward Lewis and others in fruit flies, are arranged along the chromosome in the same order as the body regions they control, and similar genes shape the human body plan too.
Epigenetics: marks on DNA

Epigenetics means changes in gene activity without changing the DNA letters. Two main marks: DNA methylation: methyl groups on cytosine usually silence a gene. Histone modification: tight or loose packing hides or exposes genes. Some marks are copied when cells divide, which keeps a liver cell a liver cell.
Small RNAs

Tiny RNA molecules (microRNA, siRNA) can block mRNA and silence genes. Andrew Fire and Craig Mello discovered RNA interference in 1998 (Nobel 2006). Ambros and Ruvkun found microRNA (Nobel 2024). Small RNAs work like a molecular 'delete' key. A short RNA pairs with a matching mRNA, and an enzyme complex then cuts it or blocks it from being read. Humans have over 2,000 microRNAs, which together help control most of our genes. RNA interference was first seen in worms, and it is now a tool in the lab and the basis of some approved drugs for rare diseases.
Famine and identical twins

People born after the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944-45 showed different methylation decades later and higher risk of some diseases. Identical twins gain different marks with age, diet and smoking. Dolly the sheep (1996) showed an adult cell's genes can be reset. Methylation means attaching a small methyl group to DNA, usually where a C is followed by a G. When a promoter is methylated, the gene tends to be silenced, like a lock on a door. Histone tags can open or close chromatin similarly. Studies of the Hunger Winter found those exposed in early pregnancy had less methylation near a growth gene (IGF2), decades later. The sequence stays the same, but the setting changes.
Watch out

Fix these Epigenetic marks are not mutations; the sequence is unchanged. Not all marks pass to children; most are erased in eggs and sperm. Epigenetics does not mean you can will your genes to change. Also, epigenetic marks are reversible, which makes them a target for some cancer drugs. X-chromosome inactivation is a clear example: in each female cell, one X is silenced by methylation and coiled up, so tortoiseshell cats show patchy colour, as Mary Lyon proposed in 1961. Also, epigenetic marks are reversible, which makes them a target for some cancer drugs. X-chromosome inactivation is a clear example: in each female cell one X is silenced by methylation and coiled up, so tortoiseshell cats show patchy colour (Mary Lyon, 1961). Lifestyle can shift marks, but not by wishing.
Cancer, diet and Indian research

Abnormal methylation can silence tumour-suppressor genes in cancers. Indian labs, including the Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology in Delhi, study gene regulation in disease. Indian population studies on diabetes link early-life nutrition to later risk, an idea called developmental programming. Hypermethylation of tumour-suppressor genes such as MLH1 is seen in some bowel cancers, and tests look for these marks in blood and stool. Epidemiology also suggests that babies born small and then well fed may be more prone to type 2 diabetes later (the 'thrifty phenotype' idea of Hales and Barker), a concern in India.
Key takeaways and questions

Cells use different genes from the same DNA. Operons (lac) are bacterial switches. Methylation and histone changes silence genes; RNAi blocks mRNA. Think about it: Why can a skin cell not simply become a neuron on its own? Why is a repressor useful for saving energy?
Mutations and Genetic Disease
Typos in the recipe

Every time DNA is copied, a few errors slip through. Most do nothing. Some cause disease. A few help survival and drive evolution. Mutations explain cancer, inherited disorders and how bacteria beat antibiotics. The human genome has about 3 billion letters, and a new baby carries around 50 to 100 new changes that neither parent had. Copying enzymes check their work, so only about one error in a billion letters survives. Think of a book copied by hand over centuries: most slips are harmless, a few spoil a sentence, and a very rare one improves it. Without variation, evolution would have nothing to choose from.
What a mutation is

A mutation is a lasting change in the DNA sequence. Germline mutations (in eggs or sperm) can be inherited. Somatic mutations (in body cells) affect only that person and cannot be passed on. Causes: copying errors, UV light, X-rays, tobacco chemicals, some viruses. A mutation in a gene's coding region may alter a protein, while one in a switch region may change how much protein is made. Hugo de Vries introduced the word 'mutation' around 1901. Mutagens are agents that raise mutation rates. UV light makes neighbouring T bases stick together; this is why sun exposure raises skin cancer risk and why the ozone layer matters. Most mutations that occur in body cells are fixed by repair or lost when the cell dies.
Small mutations (point)

Silent: new codon codes the same amino acid. Missense: a different amino acid. Sickle cell: GAG to GTG, glutamic acid to valine. Nonsense: creates a stop codon, so a short protein. Frameshift: an inserted or deleted base shifts every codon after it. Use a sentence of three-letter words as an analogy: THE CAT SAW THE DOG. A silent change swaps a word for a synonym. A missense swaps one word for another (THE HAT SAW). A nonsense puts in a full stop early. A frameshift deletes one letter, so every word after it becomes gibberish (THE ATS AWT HED OG). That is why adding or removing one or two bases is more damaging than adding three, which keeps the frame and only adds one amino acid.
Large mutations

Whole chromosome pieces can be deleted, duplicated, inverted or swapped. Whole chromosomes can be gained or lost (nondisjunction): Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome (XO), Klinefelter syndrome (XXY). Think of large mutations as editing a whole page: tearing out a paragraph (deletion), pasting it twice (duplication), turning it round (inversion) or pasting it into another chapter (translocation). The Philadelphia chromosome, a swap between chromosomes 9 and 22 found in 1960, fuses two genes and drives chronic myeloid leukaemia; the drug imatinib targets that fused protein. Extra copies of whole chromosome sets, called polyploidy, are common in plants such as wheat.
Inherited disease patterns

Autosomal recessive: need two copies, parents are carriers. Cystic fibrosis, thalassaemia, sickle cell. Autosomal dominant: one copy is enough. Huntington's disease. X-linked recessive: mostly boys. Haemophilia, colour blindness.
Repair and cancer

Cells repair DNA with proofreading and repair enzymes. Cancer develops when mutations hit genes that drive growth ( oncogenes ) or brake it ( tumour suppressors such as p53). Usually several mutations are needed. BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations raise breast and ovarian cancer risk. Repair teams are like proofreaders and a repair crew. DNA polymerase checks each new base and removes mismatches; other enzymes cut out damaged bits and fill the gap. People with xeroderma pigmentosum, who lack UV repair, develop skin cancers very early. A single mutation rarely causes cancer. Instead, a cell usually needs several hits, often over decades, which is why cancer risk rises with age. Tumour suppressors work like brakes, and oncogenes like a stuck accelerator.
From flies to bombs

Hermann Muller (1927) showed X-rays cause mutations in fruit flies (Nobel 1946). Linus Pauling (1949) called sickle cell a 'molecular disease'. Vernon Ingram (1956) traced it to one amino acid. Bruce Ames developed a test for chemicals that cause mutations in 1970s. Pauling used electrophoresis to show that sickle haemoglobin moves differently from normal haemoglobin because its charge differs, and Ingram's 'fingerprinting' found the exact amino acid. Together these linked a gene to one protein change. The Ames test, which uses bacteria that cannot make histidine, checks if a chemical makes them mutate back, and is used to screen for possible carcinogens. Muller's work is why X-ray shielding is used in clinics.
Watch out

Fix these Mutations are not always harmful; many are neutral and some are useful. Mutations do not occur 'because the organism needs them'. Carrying one copy of a recessive gene does not mean having the disease. Also, a mutation does not push a species in a planned direction. It is random with respect to need, and natural selection then sorts what survives. For example, antibiotic-resistant bacteria did not 'learn' resistance; a few already carried a helpful change, and the drug removed the rest. Also, a mutation does not push a species in a planned direction. It is random with respect to need, and natural selection then sorts what survives. Antibiotic-resistant bacteria did not 'learn' resistance; a few already carried a helpful change, and the drug removed the rest, so the resistant ones multiplied.
Sickle cell and thalassaemia

Sickle cell disease is common among tribal communities in central and western India. Carriers resist malaria, which keeps the gene frequent (balanced polymorphism). The National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) aims at screening and counselling to end it as a public health problem by 2047. Thalassaemia screening is promoted before marriage in many states.
Key takeaways and questions

Point mutations: silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift. Germline mutations are inherited; somatic are not. Cancer follows from damaged growth control genes. Think about it: Why is a frameshift usually worse than a point change? Why might carrying the sickle gene help in malarial areas? Key terms: a mutation is any lasting change in DNA; a mutagen raises the rate; a carrier has one copy of a recessive allele. Mutations are the raw material of evolution, but most are neutral. The sickle allele example is well known: carriers are partly protected from severe malaria, which keeps the allele common in malaria-prone regions, a case of balanced selection.
Biotechnology, CRISPR and GM Crops
Editing life

Insulin for diabetics, vaccines, cotton that resists bollworm and a tool that can edit a single letter of DNA all come from biotechnology. These tools are powerful and spark debates on safety, ethics and who owns seeds. Biotechnology is old and new at once: people have used yeast for bread and bacteria for curd for thousands of years. Modern biotechnology began in 1973, when Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen moved a gene from one bacterium to another using restriction enzymes (cutting like scissors) and ligase (like glue). This is recombinant DNA . It lets bacteria and yeast act as small factories for medicines and enzymes.
Recombinant DNA

In 1973 Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen moved a gene from one organism into bacteria. They used restriction enzymes (molecular scissors, found by Arber, Smith and Nathans) to cut DNA, ligase to paste it, and a plasmid as a vehicle.
Useful tools

PCR (Kary Mullis, 1983): copies a tiny DNA sample millions of times by heating and cooling cycles. Used in COVID-19 RT-PCR tests. Gel electrophoresis: sorts DNA by size. DNA sequencing: Sanger (1977); the Human Genome Project finished in 2003. PCR works in three repeating steps: heat splits the DNA strands, cooling lets short primers attach, and a heat-stable polymerase from a hot-spring bacterium builds new strands. After 30 cycles one copy becomes about a billion. Gel electrophoresis then pushes DNA through a jelly using an electric field, and small fragments move faster, like small children weaving through a crowd. Together they underlie DNA fingerprinting, invented by Alec Jeffreys in 1984, used in forensics and paternity tests.
CRISPR-Cas9

Bacteria use CRISPR as an immune memory against viruses. Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier turned it into a gene-editing tool in 2012 (Nobel 2020). A guide RNA matches a target DNA stretch. The Cas9 protein cuts the DNA there. The cell repairs the cut; scientists can disable or correct a gene. In 2023 a CRISPR therapy (Casgevy) was approved in the UK and US for sickle cell disease.
GM crops

Genetically modified crops carry genes from other species. Bt cotton holds a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that makes a protein toxic to bollworm. Golden Rice carries genes to make beta-carotene, a vitamin A source. Concerns include gene flow, pests growing resistant and corporate seed control.
Medicine and cloning

Human insulin by bacteria was marketed in 1982. Dolly the sheep (1996, Ian Wilmut) was cloned from an adult cell. Gene therapy replaces faulty genes. mRNA vaccines use the same idea of instructing cells to make a protein. Before 1982, insulin came from pig and cow pancreases. Now the human insulin gene is placed in bacteria or yeast, which make pure insulin in large tanks. For Dolly, scientists took the nucleus from a udder cell, placed it into an egg with its own nucleus removed, and used a small electric pulse to start development. It needed 277 attempts. Gene therapy first treated a child with an immune disorder in 1990, and viruses with the edited gene inside are used as delivery vans.
Safety and debate

The 1975 Asilomar conference set early safety rules. In 2018 He Jiankui announced gene-edited babies in China, widely condemned. Germline editing remains banned or tightly restricted in most countries. At Asilomar in California, scientists themselves paused some experiments until safety rules existed, an early example of responsible science. Regulators in India review GM products through the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee. Today the debates cover health, effects on other species, seed ownership, labelling, and whether gene editing of embryos should ever be allowed. The He Jiankui case led to a prison sentence in China in 2019.
Watch out

Fix these GM food is not 'DNA that infects you'; DNA is digested like any other. Gene editing is not magic; off-target edits can happen. Cloning does not copy memories or personality. Also, 'GM' is not a single thing: Bt cotton carries a bacterial gene for a protein that harms bollworm caterpillars but is harmless to people, while golden rice adds beta-carotene. Breeding has changed crops for centuries, and CRISPR can make a precise change in one letter without adding foreign DNA. Breeding has changed crops for centuries, and CRISPR can change one letter without adding foreign DNA.
India's biotech story

Khorana's 1970 gene synthesis helped found the field. Bt cotton was approved in India in 2002; it is the only GM crop allowed for commercial cultivation. GM mustard (DMH-11) was cleared by the regulator (GEAC) in 2022 but is under Supreme Court review. India's Department of Biotechnology (1986) and genome-edited rice varieties released by ICAR in 2025 show current work. Biocon and Serum Institute are major producers of insulin and vaccines.
Key takeaways and questions

Recombinant DNA: cut, paste, insert. PCR copies DNA; CRISPR edits it. GM crops like Bt cotton bring benefits and debates. Think about it: Should germline editing be allowed to prevent disease? Why or why not? How can farmers be protected from pest resistance to Bt?
Darwin and Natural Selection
The idea that explains biology

Biologist Theodosius Dobzhansky said nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution. Why antibiotics stop working, why we have an appendix and why a crow looks like a crow all follow from one simple idea. Darwin's idea is simple and testable. Individuals in a group differ; some differences are inherited; more young are born than can survive; those whose traits suit their surroundings leave more offspring. Repeat for many generations and the group changes. Think of a long sieve working slowly on a crowd, keeping what fits. Antibiotic resistance is this process happening in hospitals within years.
Descent with modification

Evolution is change in the inherited traits of populations over generations. Charles Darwin spent five years (1831-36) on HMS Beagle. Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea independently; both presented it in 1858. Darwin's book On the Origin of Species came out in 1859. Darwin's key observations came from finches and tortoises in the Galapagos Islands, where each island had its own forms, and from Thomas Malthus's essay on population, which pointed out that growth outruns food. The idea of natural selection is a mechanism, and descent with modification means all life shares ancestors, like a family tree. The theory has been refined, but not replaced, by genetics, which supplied the missing source of variation: mutation.
Natural selection in four steps
Variation: individuals differ. Inheritance: traits pass to offspring. Overproduction: more are born than survive. Differential success: those with helpful traits leave more offspring.
A worked example

The peppered moth in industrial England: before 1850 most were pale and hid on lichen. Soot darkened trees, and dark moths survived better. By 1895 dark ones dominated in Manchester. After clean air laws, pale ones returned. Bernard Kettlewell's 1950s experiments tested this. Read the peppered moth story as a chain: variation (pale and dark forms, caused by one gene), inheritance, differing survival (birds spot the moth that clashes with the tree) and a change in proportions. Kettlewell released marked moths and recaptured more of the camouflaged ones. His methods were criticised, but later studies by Majerus and others in the 2000s confirmed the main result. The gene responsible, a change near cortex , was identified in 2016.
Fitness and adaptation

'Fitness' means reproductive success, not strength. An adaptation is a trait shaped by selection. Selection acts on individuals, but populations evolve. Think of fitness as the number of surviving grandchildren, not muscle. A frail but fertile person can be 'fitter' in this sense than a strong one with no children. An adaptation is shaped for its current job: the thick fur of a polar bear, the long beak of a sunbird, the sharp thorn of a cactus. Not every feature is an adaptation, since some arise by chance or as by-products. Selection can only work on variation that already exists.
Other forces

Besides selection: mutation (new variants), genetic drift (chance changes, strong in small groups), gene flow (migration) and sexual selection (mate choice, like peacock tails). Hardy-Weinberg (1908) is the baseline for no change. Genetic drift is like drawing marbles from a jar by luck alone: a small sample can differ from the jar. A bottleneck or a few founders can change an entire population's genes, as seen in cheetahs, which have very low variation. Gene flow, such as migrants carrying genes between villages, tends to make populations alike. The Hardy-Weinberg principle tells us what to expect when none of these forces act, so any departure shows evolution at work.
Before Darwin

Lamarck (1809) proposed that traits acquired in life are inherited, such as a giraffe stretching its neck. This is wrong. Malthus (1798) on population pressure inspired Darwin. Mendel's genetics, joined with Darwin in the 1930s-40s, formed the modern synthesis. Darwin's finches in the Galapagos show beak shape tracking food: Peter and Rosemary Grant measured it over decades.
Watch out

Fix these Evolution is not 'survival of the strongest'; it is survival and reproduction of the fit for a place. Individuals do not evolve; populations do. Evolution has no goal or progress ladder. 'Theory' in science means a well-tested explanation. Also, selection acts only on what already exists. It cannot design a perfect organism, and it works with whatever variants appear, which is why the human back and the vertebrate eye have odd compromises. A scientific theory, such as the theory of gravity or of cells, is a tested framework that explains many facts.
Evolution in India

Antibiotic resistance in Indian hospitals, including NDM-1 (named for New Delhi), is selection in action. Biodiversity hotspots like the Western Ghats hold many unique species formed by long isolation. J.B.S. Haldane, who moved to India in 1957, helped found modern population genetics and worked at the Indian Statistical Institute.
Key takeaways and questions

Variation + inheritance + overproduction + differential success. Darwin and Wallace, 1858; Origin, 1859. Drift, mutation, gene flow also drive change. Think about it: How would Lamarck and Darwin each explain the giraffe's neck? Why does overusing antibiotics speed up resistance? Key terms: variation is differences between individuals, adaptation is a trait that helps survival and reproduction, and fitness is reproductive success. Lamarck proposed in 1809 that traits acquired in life are inherited, such as a giraffe stretching its neck, but experiments show that acquired body changes are not passed on through the genes.
Evidence for Evolution
Many roads, one answer

Evolution is supported by independent lines of evidence from rocks, bones, genes and living animals. When different methods point to the same story, confidence is very high. This lesson shows the main lines. Think of a detective case where fingerprints, CCTV, phone records and witnesses all point to the same person. In evolution the 'witnesses' are fossils, anatomy, embryos, DNA, geography and direct observation. Each was studied by different scientists, often by people with no wish to support Darwin, yet they agree on the tree of life. A claim that explains all of them at once is very strong.
Fossils and the rock record

Fossils are preserved remains or traces. Deeper rock is older. Radiometric dating, using the steady decay of atoms like uranium and carbon-14, gives ages in years. Earth is about 4.54 billion years old; the earliest life dates to roughly 3.5 billion years ago. Radiometric dating works like an hourglass: an unstable atom decays at a fixed rate, its half-life, so the ratio of parent to product tells the age. Carbon-14 (half-life about 5,730 years) dates remains up to about 50,000 years old, while uranium-lead dates rocks of millions to billions of years. Fossils in younger layers resemble modern life, and the oldest layers show simpler forms, in a pattern that never appears out of order. Claire Patterson fixed Earth's age in 1956 using lead in meteorites.
Transitional fossils

Archaeopteryx (1861): feathers plus reptile teeth and tail. Tiktaalik (2006): fish with a neck and wrist-like fins, about 375 million years old. Whale ancestors : Pakicetus, found in Pakistan, and Rodhocetus show legs shrinking. Transitional fossils show mixtures of traits, just as evolution predicts. Archaeopteryx lived about 150 million years ago, and many feathered dinosaurs have since been found in China. Neil Shubin and colleagues found Tiktaalik on Ellesmere Island in Canada after predicting which age of rock would hold such a fish. In India, Kutch and Himachal fossils, including Indohyus, a small deer-like relative of whales, helped trace the story of whales from land animals.
Homologous and analogous structures

Homologous: same plan, different use. The human arm, whale flipper, bat wing and horse leg share the same bones, showing common ancestry. Analogous: same use, different origin: bird and insect wings. This is convergent evolution.
Vestigial structures and embryos

Human tailbone, appendix and ear muscles are leftovers. Whales have tiny hip bones. Embryos of fish, bird and human all show gill-like pouches early on, reflecting shared ancestry (Haeckel's old 'recapitulation' idea was overstated). Vestigial structures are reduced parts that once served a larger function in ancestors, like the unused room of an old house. The human appendix may still serve a small immune role, so 'useless' is not always true. Embryos reveal that bodies are built by modifying older plans: all vertebrate embryos have a tail and pharyngeal arches, which become jaw and ear parts in humans. Karl von Baer noted these similarities in the 1820s, before Darwin.
Molecular evidence

All life uses DNA and nearly the same genetic code. The more recently two species split, the more alike their DNA and proteins. Humans and chimpanzees share about 98-99 percent of DNA sequence in aligned regions. Cytochrome c, a protein, is similar across species. DNA is a record that can be read like a manuscript copied by scribes: shared mistakes show a shared source. Humans, chimps and gorillas share broken versions of the same vitamin C gene, which we cannot use, while most other mammals make their own vitamin C. We also share many 'viral fossil' insertions in the same places in our genomes. Together these give a family tree built from molecules that matches the one built from bones.
Evolution you can watch

Bacteria become antibiotic resistant. Richard Lenski's E. coli experiment, running since 1988, has seen new traits arise over tens of thousands of generations. Insects evolve pesticide resistance. Lenski's experiment started with twelve identical flasks of bacteria. One line learned to feed on citrate, which the starting bacteria could not use, after about 31,500 generations, a new ability that arose by a chain of mutations. Antibiotic resistance, such as multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, shows the same process in hospitals. Also, mosquitoes have evolved resistance to DDT, and Galapagos finch beaks changed within years of a drought, as measured by Peter and Rosemary Grant.
Biogeography

Wallace and Darwin noted that island species resemble nearby mainland ones, and that marsupials cluster in Australia. Plate tectonics (Wegener 1912; accepted 1960s) explains why related fossils like Glossopteris appear across southern continents. Islands are natural laboratories: the finches, tortoises and mockingbirds of the Galapagos differ from island to island but resemble the South American mainland. Alfred Wallace drew a line between Asia and Australia where animal groups change abruptly. India's own story fits too: it drifted north as an island, from about 120 million years ago, and joined Asia about 50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya.

Also, 'only a theory' misunderstands science: evolution is both a fact (populations change) and a theory (natural selection and other mechanisms explain how). Fossils are never expected to be complete, since only a tiny fraction of organisms become fossils, so gaps do not weaken the evidence. Birbal Sahni and fossils

Birbal Sahni (1891-1949) was India's pioneer of palaeobotany. He studied Gondwana fossil plants, and founded the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences in Lucknow (1946, formally 1949). Shivalik hills in the north gave Ramapithecus and Sivapithecus ape fossils. Fossil whales like Indohyus from Kashmir, about 48 million years old, link whales to even-toed ungulates. Balasinor in Gujarat is a well-known dinosaur egg and fossil site.
Key takeaways and questions

Fossils, comparative anatomy, embryos, molecules and observation agree. Homologous means common ancestry; analogous means convergence. Dating shows Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. Think about it: Why are bird and bat wings analogous in some ways but homologous in others? What would disprove common ancestry?
Speciation and the Tree of Life
How one becomes many

Life on Earth has millions of species, yet all come from one common ancestor. Understanding how species split and how we group them gives a map of life, and helps in conservation and medicine. Count it: scientists have named about 2 million species, and the true total may be many millions more. Each new species begins when one population splits into two that no longer exchange genes. The 'map' is a tree, with branches for each split and the common ancestor at the base. Reading it lets doctors pick model animals, farmers find wild crop relatives, and conservationists decide which lineages are most distinct and need protecting.
What is a species?

Ernst Mayr's biological species concept (1942): a group of populations that interbreed in nature and are reproductively isolated from others. It is not perfect: it fails for asexual organisms and fossils, where shape or genes are used. Think of Mayr's definition as a test of whether two groups would act as one family. Lions and tigers can produce hybrids in captivity, yet they stay separate in the wild, so they count as distinct species. The idea fails for bacteria, which copy themselves, and for fossils, since we cannot test their mating. Carl Linnaeus, in the 1750s, started the naming system of two Latin words, such as Homo sapiens , based on shared features.
How new species form
A population is split (a river, mountain or sea). Each side faces different conditions and drifts apart genetically. Eventually they can no longer interbreed.
Reproductive barriers

Before mating: different habitat, timing, courtship or body shape. After mating: hybrids are weak or sterile. The mule (horse x donkey) is sterile. Sympatric speciation, with no barrier, happens in plants through chromosome doubling (polyploidy), and in some fish by habitat choice. Barriers act like locks on different doors. Two frog species may breed at different seasons, or sing different calls that females ignore. Even if they mate, the embryo may fail. The mule is sterile because horse and donkey differ in chromosome number (64 and 62), so the chromosomes cannot pair in meiosis. Wheat is a natural polyploid, formed by hybridisation and doubling, and is one reason a new plant species can appear in a single generation.
Adaptive radiation

When a lineage enters many open habitats it splits quickly into many forms. Darwin's finches in the Galapagos and the cichlid fishes of African lakes are classic cases. After the dinosaur extinction about 66 million years ago, mammals radiated. Think of a newly cleared field: an arriving lineage can try many ways of life without competition. Darwin's finches descend from one arrival about 2 million years ago and now include seed-crackers, insect-eaters and a blood-feeder. Cichlids in Lake Victoria produced hundreds of species in under 15,000 years. Likewise, after the asteroid impact that ended the non-bird dinosaurs, mammals expanded into new forms, from bats to whales.
The tree of life

Carolus Linnaeus (1735) gave binomial names such as Homo sapiens. Today, we use phylogenetic trees that show descent, built from DNA. Carl Woese (1977) found three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Classic ranks: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Extinction

More than 99 percent of species that ever lived are extinct. Five mass extinctions are known; the end-Permian (about 252 million years ago) killed up to 90 percent of marine species. Many scientists say we are in a sixth, driven by humans. Extinction is the normal end of species; the average lifespan of a species is roughly 1 to 10 million years. Mass extinctions are bursts where huge numbers disappear in a short geological time. The end-Cretaceous event (about 66 million years ago) followed an asteroid that struck Chicxulub, as proposed by Luis and Walter Alvarez in 1980 from iridium in rock, and the Deccan volcanoes of India may also have played a role. Current extinction rates are far above the background, due to habitat loss, hunting, invasive species and climate change.
Evidence for splits

Hawaiian fruit flies and island lizards show species forming. Ring species such as the Ensatina salamanders in California show neighbours can breed while the ends cannot. DNA clocks estimate when lineages split. Hawaii holds hundreds of fruit-fly species descended from a few colonists. Ring species show speciation in action: the Ensatina salamanders circle California's Central Valley, with neighbours interbreeding but the two ends of the ring, where they meet in the south, not mating. The molecular clock counts accumulated DNA changes, which build up at a roughly steady rate, to date splits, calibrated by fossils.

Also, 'primitive' and 'advanced' are poor words: bacteria alive today have evolved for the same length of time as we have. Carl Woese, in 1977, used rRNA to show that life has three domains and that archaea are as distinct from bacteria as from us. Also, 'primitive' and 'advanced' are poor words: bacteria alive today have evolved for as long as we have. India's species wealth

India holds about 8 percent of the world's recorded species on 2.4 percent of land. It has four biodiversity hotspots: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar). Island species, such as those on the Andaman and Nicobar islands, show allopatric speciation. The Zoological Survey of India (1916) and Botanical Survey of India (1890) document them.
Key takeaways and questions

Species: reproductively isolated groups. Isolation plus divergence leads to speciation. Three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya. Extinction is normal but is now accelerating. Think about it: Why do islands have so many unique species? Why is a mule sterile although it is healthy? Key terms: allopatric speciation follows geographic separation; sympatric occurs in the same area. Reproductive isolation keeps gene pools apart, and adaptive radiation is a burst of new forms. In the tree, clades are a common ancestor with all its descendants. Islands hold many unique species because small, isolated populations diverge by selection and drift.
Human Evolution
Our own family tree

Where did we come from? The answer is not a single line from ape to human but a bushy tree of many human-like species, most now extinct. Fossils and DNA tell a story that is still being written. Think of a bush, not a ladder. At several times, more than one human-like species lived at once. The Neanderthals and our own species overlapped for thousands of years. Most branches ended without descendants. We know the story from bones, stone tools, footprints and, since the 1990s, from ancient DNA, a field pioneered by Svante Paabo (Nobel 2022).
Humans are apes

Humans belong to the primates and the great apes. Our closest living relatives are chimpanzees and bonobos. Humans and chimps share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 7 million years ago. This is a cousin relationship, not descent. Saying 'humans are apes' is a statement about the tree: we sit inside the great ape branch, together with orangutans, gorillas and chimps, and are placed with them because of shared features such as no tail and a flexible shoulder. The split from chimps was followed by a long line of upright, bipedal species. Our chromosome 2 is a fusion of two ape chromosomes, a fact visible in our DNA and confirming that we share ancestors with other apes.
Walking upright first

Bipedalism came before big brains. Sahelanthropus (about 7 million years ago) may be early. Australopithecus afarensis , the famed 'Lucy' (found by Donald Johanson in Ethiopia, 1974, about 3.2 million years old), walked upright but had a small brain.
The genus Homo

Homo habilis (about 2.4 mya): early tools. Homo erectus (from about 1.9 mya): used fire, travelled to Asia. Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis): in Europe and Asia; large brain, buried dead. Homo sapiens : appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago (Jebel Irhoud, Morocco). Homo erectus was the first to leave Africa, with remains in Java and China, and it used fire and made hand axes. Homo sapiens spread from Africa, probably from about 70,000 years ago, and reached India. Meanwhile Neanderthals, of whom many Europeans and Asians carry 1 to 2 percent DNA, were our cousins, as shown by genome work in 2010. A Denisovan genome from a Siberian cave was also read, and some Asian and Pacific peoples carry its traces. Homo floresiensis, a small relative on Flores, lived until about 50,000 years ago.
Out of Africa

Genetic data show modern humans left Africa in waves, at least by about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago, and replaced or mixed with other humans. Non-African people carry 1-2 percent Neanderthal DNA; some Asians carry Denisovan DNA. Svante Paabo won the 2022 Nobel for sequencing ancient DNA.
Brain, tools and culture

Brain size grew from about 450 cc (Australopithecus) to about 1350 cc (us). Tools, cooking, speech and social learning pushed this. Cultural evolution (agriculture about 10,000 years ago) now moves faster than genetic change. The 'expensive tissue' idea says that the brain uses about 20 percent of our energy, so cooking, which makes food easier to digest, may have helped our brains grow. Walking upright freed the hands for tools, and stone tools date back over 3 million years. Language and teaching let knowledge be stored in groups, so each generation starts where the last stopped. Agriculture began independently in several places, including the Indus region, around 9,000 years ago.
Fossils and DNA

Raymond Dart found the Taung child in 1924. Louis and Mary Leakey worked in Olduvai Gorge. Mitochondrial DNA studies (Cann, Stoneking and Wilson, 1987) pointed to an African origin. Homo naledi (2015, South Africa) and Homo floresiensis (2003, Indonesia) show we shared the world with other humans.

Narmada Man, a skull found at Hathnora (1982, Arun Sonakia) has been linked to early Homo. Stone tools at Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu date to about 385,000 years ago.
