Humans and chimps share a common ancestor 6-7 mya. Upright walking came before big brains. Homo sapiens arose in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Our DNA records mixing with Neanderthals and Denisovans. Think about it: Why does a bushy tree fit the evidence better than a ladder? What does Neanderthal DNA in modern people tell us?
Digestion and Nutrition
From plate to cells

Food is too big to enter your blood. Digestion breaks it into tiny molecules that can. Knowing the steps explains acidity, lactose intolerance, why fibre matters and why malnutrition remains a big issue. The gut is really a long tube, about 9 metres from mouth to anus, that is technically 'outside' the body. Food must be broken down twice over: mechanically (chewing, churning) and chemically (enzymes). Only then can the small molecules be absorbed: starch into glucose, protein into amino acids, and fat into fatty acids. William Beaumont studied digestion directly in the 1820s through a soldier's stomach wound.
The journey
The digestive tract is a long tube, about 9 metres, with helpers (liver, pancreas, gall bladder). Digestion is both mechanical (chewing, churning) and chemical (enzymes).
Mouth and stomach

Salivary amylase breaks starch into sugars (chew roti long enough and it tastes sweet). The stomach makes hydrochloric acid (pH about 2) that kills germs, and pepsin that cuts proteins. A mucus layer protects the wall. William Beaumont studied digestion through a gunshot wound in Alexis St Martin's stomach in the 1820s.
Small intestine

Bile from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) breaks fat into droplets. The pancreas sends enzymes: amylase, trypsin and lipase. The wall makes more enzymes. The lining has finger-like villi that give a surface of roughly a tennis court for absorption of sugars, amino acids and fatty acids into blood and lymph.
Large intestine and gut microbes

It absorbs water and salts and forms faeces. Trillions of bacteria help make vitamin K and some B vitamins and break fibre. Gut microbes now link to immunity and mood. The large intestine is about 1.5 metres long and takes the leftovers, mostly water, fibre and dead cells. It reclaims roughly a litre or more of water a day, which is why severe diarrhoea is dangerous: water is lost before it can be absorbed. Gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids that feed the cells of the gut wall. Antibiotics can disturb this community, and a probiotic like curd may help restore it.
Nutrients you need

Carbohydrates: main fuel. Proteins: building and repair. Fats: energy, cell membranes, vitamins A, D, E, K. Vitamins and minerals: small amounts, big roles. Iron for blood; iodine for thyroid; vitamin D for bones. Fibre and water. Think of a balanced thali as a toolkit: rice or roti for fuel, dal for protein, vegetables for vitamins and fibre, and a little ghee or oil for fat-soluble vitamins. About 20 amino acids build our proteins, and nine are 'essential', meaning we must eat them. Iodised salt protects the thyroid, and milk, sunlight and fish give vitamin D. Water makes up about 60 percent of body weight.
Deficiency diseases

Lack of vitamin C causes scurvy (James Lind showed lime helped sailors, 1747). Vitamin D lack gives rickets. Vitamin A lack leads to night blindness. Iron lack leads to anaemia. Protein-energy lack gives kwashiorkor and marasmus. These diseases are the reverse of a well-planned diet. James Lind tested citrus fruit on sailors in 1747, in one of the first controlled trials, long before vitamin C was discovered. Anaemia is very common in India, especially among women and children, and is addressed with iron-folic acid tablets and fortified foods. Kwashiorkor, with swollen belly, comes from too little protein; marasmus, with wasting, from too little food overall.
Discovering vitamins

Christiaan Eijkman (1890s) found that unpolished rice prevented beriberi in fowl; Frederick Hopkins and Casimir Funk worked on 'vital amines' in the 1910s. Ivan Pavlov (1890s) studied digestive reflexes. H. pylori, found by Marshall and Warren (1982), causes most stomach ulcers, not stress. Eijkman's chickens fed polished rice developed a paralysis like beriberi, and brown rice cured them; Hopkins showed in 1912 that milk contained 'accessory food factors'. Pavlov won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on digestive glands. Barry Marshall even drank a culture of H. pylori to prove his point, and he and Robin Warren shared the 2005 Nobel Prize. Ulcers are now treated with antibiotics.
Watch out

Fix these Ulcers are mainly from H. pylori and painkillers, not spicy food alone. Most absorption is in the small intestine, not the stomach. Fat is not 'bad'; the type and amount matter. Also, 'acidity' is not always too much acid: stomach acid (pH about 1.5 to 2) is needed to kill germs and activate pepsin, and the stomach lining is protected by a layer of mucus. Digestion does not start in the stomach, either: salivary amylase starts on starch in the mouth. Fibre cannot be digested, but it keeps the gut moving.
Nutrition programmes

India runs the Integrated Child Development Services (1975), Mid-Day Meal (now PM POSHAN) and the National Food Security Act (2013). Anaemia remains widespread among women and children. Iodised salt (National Goitre Control Programme, 1962) cut iodine deficiency. Millets are promoted as 'Shree Anna' after 2023, the International Year of Millets.
Key takeaways and questions

Mouth, stomach, small and large intestine do different jobs. Villi increase absorption area. Enzymes: amylase (starch), pepsin and trypsin (protein), lipase (fat). Deficiencies cause specific diseases. Think about it: Why does bile not digest fat chemically but still help? Why do we need pH 2 in the stomach but not in the intestine?
Circulation and the Heart
A pump that never rests

Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day, moving roughly 5 litres of blood per minute at rest. Every cell needs oxygen and food delivered and waste removed. Heart disease is India's leading cause of death, so this one is useful to know. The heart is a muscle about the size of your fist, and it beats without tiring, because cardiac muscle cells are packed with mitochondria. Over an average lifetime it beats about 2.5 billion times. It works as two pumps side by side: the right side sends blood to the lungs, the left sends blood to the rest of the body. A person's blood vessels, laid end to end, would stretch about 100,000 km.
Blood and vessels

Blood has red cells (carry oxygen using haemoglobin), white cells (defence), platelets (clotting) and plasma (liquid). Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; veins bring it back, with valves; capillaries are thin walls where exchange happens. Blood makes up around 7 to 8 percent of body weight, about 5 litres in an adult. Red cells have no nucleus, which leaves room for haemoglobin, and each lives about 120 days. Arteries have thick, elastic walls to take each pulse, like a garden hose that can stretch. Veins have thinner walls and one-way valves, so blood does not slip back under gravity, which matters most in the legs. Capillaries are one cell thick, so oxygen and nutrients can pass through easily.
The four chambers

The human heart has two atria (receive) and two ventricles (pump). The right side handles blood without oxygen; the left side handles blood with oxygen. Valves keep flow one-way, making the 'lub-dub' sound.
Double circulation

Blood passes through the heart twice per full round. The pulmonary circuit goes heart to lungs and back. The systemic circuit goes heart to body and back. This keeps oxygen-rich and poor blood apart and lets the body get high pressure. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps to the whole body.
The heartbeat

The heart has its own pacemaker, the sino-atrial (SA) node , which sends electrical signals across the atria, then through the AV node to the ventricles. An ECG records this. Blood pressure is written like 120/80 mmHg (systolic over diastolic). Nerves and hormones such as adrenaline change the rate.
Disease and clotting

Fat (cholesterol) deposits narrow arteries (atherosclerosis). A blocked coronary artery causes a heart attack. Blood clots are formed when platelets and fibrin seal a wound; vitamin K helps. High BP, smoking, diabetes and inactivity raise risk. Atherosclerosis starts when damaged artery walls collect cholesterol and immune cells, forming a plaque, like limescale narrowing a pipe. If a plaque cracks, a clot can form and block the artery. Clotting is a chain of steps in which platelets stick together and the protein fibrinogen becomes sticky fibrin threads, like a mesh. Eating less salt and saturated fat, not smoking, staying active and checking blood pressure reduce risk, and South Asians develop heart disease at younger ages on average.
From Harvey to open-heart

William Harvey (1628) showed that blood circulates, rather than being used up. Marcello Malpighi (1661) saw capillaries. Karl Landsteiner (1901) discovered ABO blood groups. Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant in 1967. Before Harvey, people followed Galen's idea from the second century that the liver made blood and the body used it up. Harvey counted that the heart pumps far more blood in an hour than the body could ever make, so it must go round in a circle. He could not see capillaries, which Malpighi later saw with a microscope. Landsteiner's blood groups made safe transfusion possible, and the first heart transplant patient, Louis Washkansky, lived 18 days.
Watch out

Fix these Arteries do not always carry oxygen-rich blood; the pulmonary artery does not. The heart is on the left only in feel; it sits mostly mid-chest. Heart attack differs from cardiac arrest (electrical failure). Also, blood is not blue inside the body: veins look blue through the skin, but blood is always red, darker when it has less oxygen. A heart attack is a plumbing problem (a blocked artery), while cardiac arrest is an electrical problem, when the heart stops pumping effectively. CPR can help in both. Also, blood is not blue inside the body: veins look blue through the skin, but blood is always red, darker when it carries less oxygen. A heart attack is a plumbing problem (a blocked artery), while cardiac arrest is an electrical problem, when the heart stops pumping effectively. CPR can help in both.
India's heart story

The first successful heart transplant in India was done by Dr P. Venugopal at AIIMS, Delhi, in 1994. Dr Devi Shetty pioneered low-cost cardiac surgery. The National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases covers hypertension screening, and Indians show earlier heart disease than many populations.
Key takeaways and questions

Heart: 4 chambers, double circulation. Arteries away, veins back, capillaries exchange. SA node is the pacemaker. Atherosclerosis causes heart attacks. Think about it: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker? Why are valves needed in veins but not in arteries? Key terms: systole is contraction and diastole is relaxation, so a reading of 120/80 mmHg gives the pressure at each. The heart's own blood supply comes through the coronary arteries. The double circulation means blood passes through the heart twice per round trip, which keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood apart and lets the body get high pressure.
Breathing and the Lungs
Two jobs, one system

Breathing feels automatic, yet it is the link between the air and every cell's energy factory. The lungs bring oxygen in and carbon dioxide out. India's air pollution and TB make this system a major public health topic. Each day you take about 20,000 breaths and move around 10,000 litres of air. Air is warmed, moistened and filtered by the nose, with tiny hairs and mucus trapping dust. The system also helps with speech, smell and keeping blood acidity steady. In India, tuberculosis, which spreads through droplets, and fine-particle air pollution (PM2.5) both strongly affect lung health.
The path of air

Air enters the nose (warmed, filtered), passes the pharynx, larynx (voice box) and trachea (windpipe, held open by cartilage rings), then branches into two bronchi, many bronchioles and ends in tiny sacs called alveoli .
How we breathe in and out

Breathing is driven by pressure. Inhale: the diaphragm flattens and ribs rise, so the chest grows. Pressure drops and air rushes in. Exhale: muscles relax, the chest shrinks, and air is pushed out. The medulla in the brain controls rate, mostly triggered by rising CO2, not low oxygen.
Gas exchange

About 300-500 million alveoli give a surface of roughly 70 square metres. Their walls and neighbouring capillaries are one cell thick. Oxygen moves into blood and carbon dioxide moves out by simple diffusion, driven by differences in partial pressure. Imagine a lung as an upside-down tree whose twigs end in tiny grape-like air sacs. Spread flat, the alveolar surface would cover about a third of a tennis court. Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries, and the gases only travel the width of two thin cells, about 0.5 micrometre. A thin film of fluid inside, with surfactant , keeps the sacs from collapsing. Premature babies sometimes lack surfactant.
Carrying gases

About 97 percent of oxygen rides on haemoglobin in red cells. Carbon dioxide travels mostly as bicarbonate in plasma, with some on haemoglobin and some dissolved. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, which is why it is so dangerous. Each red cell holds about 270 million haemoglobin molecules, and each molecule can carry four oxygen molecules, one on each iron-containing haem group. Haemoglobin picks up oxygen in the lungs, where oxygen is plentiful, and releases it in active tissues, where oxygen is low and CO2 and acid are high. Carbon dioxide forms bicarbonate with the help of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. People living at high altitude, such as in Ladakh, adapt with more red cells or other changes.
Lung volumes

A normal breath moves about 500 ml (tidal volume). Total lung capacity is roughly 5-6 litres, and vital capacity (largest breath out) about 3.5-4.5 litres. A spirometer measures these. Even after the biggest breath out, about 1.2 litres of air stays in the lungs (residual volume), so the alveoli never fully collapse. Vital capacity depends on height, age, sex and fitness, and a trained swimmer may have a larger one. A spirometer records a person's breath as a graph, and doctors use it to diagnose asthma and COPD by measuring how fast one can blow out.
Respiratory science

Lavoisier (1780s) linked breathing to burning. Christian Bohr (1904) showed CO2 helps haemoglobin release oxygen (Bohr effect). Smoking's link to lung cancer was shown by Doll and Hill in 1950. Lavoisier's insight in the 1780s showed that air contains a gas that is used up; Joseph Priestley had earlier found oxygen in 1774. Bohr's effect (the father of the physicist Niels Bohr) explains why working muscles, which make CO2 and acid, get extra oxygen. Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill followed thousands of British doctors and found that smokers died of lung cancer far more often.
Watch out

Fix these Lungs do not have muscles; the diaphragm and rib muscles do the work. Exhaled air still has about 16 percent oxygen, which makes mouth-to-mouth rescue possible. The urge to breathe comes from CO2 rise. When you breathe in, the diaphragm flattens and the rib muscles lift the ribs, making the chest bigger and pressure inside lower, so air flows in, as in a bellows. Breathing out at rest is mostly passive recoil. The rise of carbon dioxide, not the fall of oxygen, is the main trigger that sensors in the brainstem use to control breathing rate.
Air pollution and TB

India has the largest TB burden in the world; the national goal is to end TB by 2025, later extended, under the National TB Elimination Programme. Many Indian cities have high PM2.5 levels, tied to asthma and COPD. The National Clean Air Programme (2019) targets cuts in particle levels. Indian yogic breathing (pranayama) has been studied for effects on lung function.
Key takeaways and questions

Air path: nose, trachea, bronchi, alveoli. The diaphragm creates pressure change. Exchange by diffusion in alveoli. Haemoglobin carries oxygen; CO binds too tightly. Think about it: Why are alveoli so numerous and thin? Why does holding breath become unbearable? Key terms: inspiration is breathing in and expiration is breathing out. The pleural membranes wrap each lung with a thin fluid layer that lets it glide. Smoking damages the cilia that sweep out mucus and causes emphysema, where alveoli break down and surface area falls. Remember that the exchange of gases happens only in the alveoli, not in the bronchi.
The Nervous System and the Brain
Your body's wiring

Reading this sentence uses about 86 billion neurons. The nervous system senses the world, decides and acts in milliseconds. Epilepsy, Parkinson's, depression and stroke are all problems of this network. A neuron is a cell built to carry signals. A dendrite receives them, the cell body adds them up, and a long axon sends them on, like a wire with branches. The brain weighs about 1.4 kg yet uses around 20 percent of the body's energy. Santiago Ramon y Cajal showed in the 1880s and 1890s that the nervous system is made of separate cells, and shared the 1906 Nobel Prize with Camillo Golgi.
The neuron

A neuron has dendrites (receive signals), a cell body and an axon (sends signals). Many axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty sheath that speeds signals up to about 100 m/s. Santiago Ramon y Cajal (1890s) showed the brain is made of separate cells, not a continuous net.
The nerve impulse

Resting: the inside is negative, about -70 mV, kept by the Na+/K+ pump. Stimulus: sodium channels open, Na+ rushes in, inside turns positive (depolarisation). Recovery: potassium channels open, K+ leaves, resting state returns. The wave moves down the axon. It is all-or-none. Hodgkin and Huxley described this in the squid giant axon (1952, Nobel 1963).
The synapse

Neurons do not touch. At a synapse, the signal triggers release of a chemical neurotransmitter (acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, GABA) that crosses a gap about 20 nm wide and excites or inhibits the next cell. Otto Loewi's frog heart experiment (1921) showed chemical transmission. Imagine passing a note across a small stream: the signal arrives at the end of the axon, opens calcium gates, and vesicles of neurotransmitter fuse with the membrane and spill into the gap. The molecules attach to receptors on the next cell, and are then removed or broken down by enzymes so the message stops. Many drugs act here: antidepressants such as SSRIs raise serotonin, and nerve gases block acetylcholine breakdown. Parkinson's disease follows loss of dopamine-making cells.
Organisation

Central nervous system: brain and spinal cord. Peripheral: nerves to the body, split into somatic (voluntary) and autonomic (involuntary; sympathetic 'fight or flight' and parasympathetic 'rest and digest'). The sympathetic system is like pressing the accelerator: the heart speeds up, pupils widen and digestion slows. The parasympathetic system is the brake, slowing the heart and encouraging digestion. The spinal cord, protected inside the vertebrae, carries messages up and down, and about 31 pairs of spinal nerves branch from it. Sensory neurons carry information toward the CNS, and motor neurons carry commands away from it.
The brain's parts

Cerebrum: thought, senses, voluntary action, memory. Cerebellum: balance and coordination. Brainstem (medulla): breathing, heart rate. Hypothalamus: body temperature, hunger, hormones. The cerebrum has two halves joined by the corpus callosum, and its folded outer layer, the cortex , is about 2 to 4 mm thick and has lobes for vision (occipital), hearing and memory (temporal), movement and touch (frontal and parietal). Phineas Gage, a railway worker injured in 1848, changed in personality after an iron rod passed through his frontal lobe, hinting at its role. The hippocampus helps form new memories, as seen in the patient known as H.M. in the 1950s.
Reflex arc

A reflex is a fast automatic response: touch a hot pan and the signal goes sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron, muscle. The brain only hears about it later. The reflex arc is a shortcut that skips the brain and is therefore fast, as little as 30 milliseconds, protecting you from injury. The knee-jerk is a simple one that doctors test with a small hammer, using only two neurons. The spinal cord acts as the control centre, and at the same time it passes a message up so you feel the pain a moment later. Not all reflexes are inborn: Pavlov showed that animals can learn conditioned reflexes.
Brain mapping

Paul Broca (1861) linked speech to the left frontal area after studying a patient called Tan. Phineas Gage's 1848 injury hinted at the frontal lobe's role in personality. Wilder Penfield mapped the cortex in the 1930s-50s. Today fMRI shows active regions. Patient H.M. (1953) revealed the hippocampus's role in forming memories.
Watch out

Fix these We use all of the brain, not 10 percent. Neurons can be formed in some brain areas in adults (neurogenesis in the hippocampus), though limited. Left-brain and right-brain personality types are mostly a myth. Brain scans show that activity occurs throughout the brain across a day, even in sleep. The idea of 'left-brained' and 'right-brained' people comes from real findings that language is mostly processed on the left in most people, but the two halves work together constantly. Roger Sperry's work on 'split-brain' patients earned a Nobel Prize in 1981, and showed that each half has special skills.
India's brain health work

NIMHANS in Bengaluru is a premier institute for mental health and neurosciences. The National Mental Health Programme began in 1982 and the Mental Healthcare Act came in 2017. J.C. Bose's plant studies on electrical signals were a pioneering idea in his time. Indian neuroscientists such as Vilayanur Ramachandran (born in Tamil Nadu) became known worldwide for work on phantom limbs.
Key takeaways and questions

Neuron: dendrite, body, axon. Impulse: Na+ in, K+ out, all-or-none. Synapse: chemical messengers. Cerebrum thinks, cerebellum balances, medulla keeps vital functions. Think about it: Why does myelin make signals faster? How could a drug that blocks neurotransmitter breakdown change mood? Key terms: an impulse (action potential) is a wave of sodium ions rushing in and then potassium ions out, travelling at up to about 120 metres per second in myelinated nerves. Myelin , a fatty sheath, lets the signal jump between gaps called nodes of Ranvier, so it is faster. Multiple sclerosis damages myelin. Hodgkin and Huxley worked this out in giant squid axons in 1952.
Hormones and the Endocrine System
Slow messages, big effects

Nerves are fast text messages; hormones are letters sent by blood. They control growth, mood, sugar levels, puberty and stress. Diabetes, thyroid disease and growth disorders are hormone problems, and all are common in India. A hormone is a chemical made by a gland and released into the blood, where it reaches every cell but acts only on cells with the matching receptor, like a radio signal that only the right set picks up. Ernest Starling coined the word 'hormone' in 1905 after finding secretin in the gut. Because blood is slow, hormones suit long jobs such as growth and metabolism. Feedback loops, like a thermostat, keep levels steady.
What a hormone is

Hormones are chemical messengers made by glands and carried in blood to target cells that have matching receptors. William Bayliss and Ernest Starling coined the word in 1905 after discovering secretin. Control is usually by negative feedback .
Pituitary: the master gland

A pea-sized gland under the brain. It makes growth hormone (too little: dwarfism; too much: gigantism), TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin, and stores ADH and oxytocin from the hypothalamus. ADH helps the kidney save water. The pituitary hangs from the hypothalamus, which links the nervous and hormone systems. The hypothalamus sends releasing hormones to the front of the pituitary, which then signals the thyroid, adrenals and gonads, a chain of command. The back of the pituitary stores oxytocin, which helps in birth and milk release. Too little ADH causes diabetes insipidus, with large volumes of dilute urine, which is different from diabetes mellitus.
Thyroid and calcium

The thyroid makes thyroxine, which sets metabolism and needs iodine. Lack of iodine causes goitre. Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium; calcitonin lowers it. Thyroxine acts like a throttle on the body's engine. Too little makes a person slow, cold and tired (hypothyroidism); too much speeds everything up (hyperthyroidism). Without iodine, the thyroid enlarges into a goitre. India's iodised salt programme, begun in the 1960s, greatly reduced goitre. Parathyroid and calcitonin together keep blood calcium within a narrow range, which nerves, muscles and clotting need. The body keeps blood calcium steady within a narrow band. In India, vitamin D deficiency is common despite sunshine, so many people are checked for it. Thyroid disorders are also frequent, and a simple blood test for TSH helps diagnose them.
Blood sugar: insulin and glucagon

After a meal, the pancreas releases insulin , which makes cells absorb glucose and liver store glycogen. Between meals, glucagon releases glucose. In type 1 diabetes the body makes no insulin; in type 2 cells respond poorly. Banting and Best (1921, Toronto) isolated insulin; Banting and Macleod got the 1923 Nobel.
Adrenal glands and stress

The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline in seconds: heart races, glucose rises. The cortex releases cortisol (long stress) and aldosterone (salt balance). Chronic stress keeps cortisol high and harms health. Walter Cannon called adrenaline's effect 'fight or flight': heart rate and breathing rise, blood moves to muscles, and the liver releases glucose. Cortisol takes hours to act and also suppresses inflammation, so related drugs (steroids) are used for allergies and swelling. Hans Selye described the body's general stress response in the 1930s. Aldosterone tells the kidney to hold sodium, which pulls water and raises blood pressure.
Sex hormones and others

Testes make testosterone; ovaries make oestrogen and progesterone. Melatonin from the pineal gland sets sleep rhythm. Plants also use hormones: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, ethylene and abscisic acid. At puberty, signals from the brain tell the gonads to make sex hormones, which cause the growth of body hair, a deeper voice or the start of the menstrual cycle. Melatonin rises in darkness, and bright light at night, such as from phone screens, can delay it. Plant hormones work much the same way: auxin moves down a shoot's shaded side and makes it bend toward light, and ethylene from one ripe banana can hasten ripening of its neighbours.
Early experiments

Arnold Berthold (1849) moved a rooster's testes and found comb and behaviour preserved, hinting at chemical signals. Banting's dog experiments led to insulin. Radioimmunoassay (Yalow, 1977 Nobel) allowed hormone measurement. Berthold's rooster is often cited as the first endocrine experiment: transplanted testes in a new place still worked, so something carried in the blood, not nerves, must be responsible. In 1921, Frederick Banting and Charles Best, in John Macleod's lab at Toronto, extracted insulin from dog pancreas, and in 1922 the first patient, a boy of 14, was treated. Yalow and Berson's radioimmunoassay measured tiny amounts of hormones in blood.
Watch out

Fix these Hormones are not only sex hormones. Type 2 diabetes is not just 'eating sugar'; genes, weight and activity matter. Insulin is not a cure but a replacement. Insulin lowers blood sugar by helping cells take up glucose; glucagon, from the same pancreas, raises it. In type 1 diabetes the body's own immune cells destroy the insulin-making cells; in type 2, cells respond poorly to insulin. India has among the world's largest numbers of people with diabetes. Also, 'hormone imbalance' is not an explanation for every symptom; doctors test levels before concluding.
The diabetes capital

India has more than 100 million people with diabetes, among the highest in the world. Indians develop it at lower body weight, linked to belly fat and genes. The National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases covers diabetes screening. Iodised salt helps fight goitre. India makes much of the world's low-cost insulin.
Key takeaways and questions

Hormones travel in blood to targets; slower but longer lasting. Negative feedback keeps levels steady. Insulin lowers, glucagon raises blood sugar. Pituitary directs many glands. Think about it: Why does a high thyroxine level reduce TSH? How do nerve and hormone signals differ in speed and duration?
Immunity and Vaccines
Your inner army

Germs surround us, yet most of the time we stay healthy. Vaccines have wiped out smallpox and nearly polio. Understanding immunity explains allergies, transplants rejection, HIV and how vaccines are built. The immune system has two tiers. Innate immunity is quick and general: skin, stomach acid, mucus, and white cells such as neutrophils and macrophages that swallow invaders. Adaptive immunity is slower but learns and remembers, like a guard dog that is first trained on a scent. Edward Jenner in 1796 used cowpox to protect against smallpox, and the word 'vaccine' comes from vacca , Latin for cow.
Two layers of defence
Innate immunity is fast and general: skin, mucus, stomach acid, fever, inflammation and cells that eat germs (macrophages, neutrophils). Adaptive immunity is slower but specific and has memory.
The adaptive response

Antigen-presenting cells show pieces of the germ. Helper T cells sound the alarm. B cells make antibodies that stick to the germ (humoral immunity). Killer T cells destroy infected cells (cell-mediated). Memory cells remain for years. Think of it as a well-run army. Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that lock on to a particular antigen like a key in a lock, marking the germ for destruction or blocking it from entering cells. Each B cell makes one type of antibody, and the right one multiplies in a process called clonal selection , proposed by Macfarlane Burnet in the 1950s. Killer T cells find infected cells by the bits of germ displayed on their surface and trigger them to die.
Primary and secondary response

The first meeting with a germ is slow (about a week). The second is faster and stronger, since memory cells are ready. This is what a vaccine exploits. This is why you rarely get chickenpox or measles twice. After the first infection, memory B and T cells wait, sometimes for decades. On the second meeting, antibody levels rise within days and reach a far higher peak, usually before symptoms appear. A booster dose works like a second meeting, so protection from some vaccines (like tetanus) needs repeating every ten years or so.
How vaccines work

A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version of a germ. Types: weakened live (measles, OPV), killed (IPV), parts or proteins (hepatitis B), toxoid (tetanus) and mRNA (some COVID-19 vaccines). When most people are immune, herd immunity protects the rest. Edward Jenner (1796) used cowpox to protect against smallpox; Pasteur extended it to rabies (1885).
When immunity misfires

Allergy: over-reaction to harmless things. Autoimmune disease: attacks self (type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis). HIV destroys helper T cells, causing AIDS. Transplants need matching since the body attacks foreign tissue. In an allergy, the body makes IgE antibodies against pollen or peanuts, and mast cells then release histamine, causing sneezing, itching or, rarely, a dangerous shock (anaphylaxis). In an autoimmune disease, the system loses its ability to tell self from non-self, and attacks joints, the thyroid or insulin-making cells. HIV, identified in 1983 by Luc Montagnier and Francoise Barre-Sinoussi, targets helper T cells, so ordinary infections turn severe. Antiretroviral drugs now keep the virus under control.
Antibodies and Nobel work

Emil von Behring and Kitasato (1890) found antitoxin serum. Paul Ehrlich and Elie Metchnikoff shared the 1908 Nobel. Medawar showed tolerance. Kohler and Milstein created monoclonal antibodies in 1975. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980. Behring and Kitasato showed that blood serum from an animal given small doses of diphtheria toxin could protect another animal, the first 'passive' immunity, and Behring won the first Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1901. Metchnikoff discovered phagocytes, and Ehrlich explained antibodies. Monoclonal antibodies, from one B-cell line, are now used against cancers and autoimmune diseases. Smallpox, a disease with high death rates, was eradicated after a global campaign led by the WHO, and India's last case was in 1975.
Watch out

Fix these Vaccines do not cause the disease they protect against (killed or part vaccines cannot). Antibiotics do not work against viruses. A runny nose does not prove a weak immune system. Also, vaccines teach the body without causing the disease: some contain killed germs, some a weakened live form, some only a protein piece, and some mRNA instructions. Rare side effects occur, but are far smaller than the risks of the diseases. 'Herd immunity' protects people who cannot be vaccinated when most others are immune. Also, vaccines teach the body without causing the disease: some contain killed germs, some a weakened live form, some only a protein piece, and some mRNA instructions. Rare side effects occur, but are far smaller than the risks of the diseases. 'Herd immunity' protects people who cannot be vaccinated when most others are immune. Antibiotics also do not 'boost' immunity.
From smallpox to polio and COVID

India's last smallpox case was in 1975, and the country was certified polio-free by WHO in 2014 after the Pulse Polio drive (1995). The Universal Immunisation Programme (1985) covers children and mothers; Mission Indradhanush (2014) reaches missed children. During COVID-19, Covaxin (Bharat Biotech with ICMR) and Covishield (Serum Institute) were used, and over two billion doses were given in India.
Key takeaways and questions

Innate: fast, general. Adaptive: specific, memory. B cells make antibodies; T cells coordinate and kill. Vaccines train memory without disease. HIV targets helper T cells. Think about it: Why do booster doses help? Why does herd immunity protect a baby too young to be vaccinated?
Reproduction and Development
How a single cell becomes a person

Nine months turn one fertilised cell into a baby with trillions of cells. Understanding reproduction supports health education, family planning and the treatment of infertility, a matter that affects millions of couples in India. Human development takes about 38 weeks from fertilisation. In the first 8 weeks the organism is called an embryo and most organs form; after that it is a foetus and the organs grow and mature. Because organs form early, harmful drugs or infections such as rubella, and also alcohol, are most dangerous in the first trimester. Folic acid before and in early pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida.
Gametes

Sperm (male) and eggs (female) are haploid cells made by meiosis. Sperm are made in the testes and travel through the epididymis and vas deferens. Eggs mature in the ovaries ; a girl is born with about a million immature eggs and typically about 400 are released in life.
The menstrual cycle

About 28 days, controlled by hormones. Days 1-5: menstruation (the lining sheds). FSH grows a follicle; oestrogen rebuilds the lining. Day 14: an LH surge causes ovulation . Progesterone from the corpus luteum prepares the uterus. If no pregnancy, hormone levels fall and the cycle restarts.
Fertilisation to implantation
The sperm meets the egg in the fallopian tube. Fusion makes a zygote (2n). It divides (cleavage) into a ball of cells, the blastocyst, which implants in the uterine wall at about day 6-7.
Pregnancy and the placenta

The placenta passes oxygen and nutrients from mother to foetus and waste back, without mixing the bloods. It also makes hormones (hCG, which pregnancy tests detect). Pregnancy lasts about 38 weeks from fertilisation. Organs form in the first 8 weeks, the most sensitive period for drugs and viruses.
Birth and lactation

Oxytocin triggers contractions. After birth, prolactin makes milk and oxytocin lets it flow. Early breast milk (colostrum) is rich in antibodies. Late in pregnancy the baby's head presses on the cervix, which sends a signal to the brain to release oxytocin, which strengthens contractions, which push the baby harder: a positive feedback loop that ends at birth. Colostrum is thick and yellowish and gives the newborn protective antibodies (IgA) and is easy to digest. The WHO advises feeding only breast milk for the first six months, and suckling itself keeps prolactin and oxytocin flowing.
Contraception and infertility

Methods include barriers (condoms), hormonal pills, copper-T, and sterilisation. In vitro fertilisation (IVF) makes an embryo outside the body; the first IVF baby, Louise Brown, was born in 1978 (Robert Edwards, Nobel 2010). Barrier methods like condoms also help prevent sexually transmitted infections, which pills and the copper-T do not. Pills use oestrogen and progesterone to prevent ovulation, and the copper-T prevents implantation and harms sperm. In IVF, eggs are collected after hormone stimulation, mixed with sperm in a dish, and a healthy embryo is placed in the uterus a few days later. In India, Subhash Mukhopadhyay reported the world's second IVF baby in Kolkata in 1978, a story long overlooked.
Development discoveries

Karl Ernst von Baer found the mammalian egg (1827). Hans Spemann and Hilde Mangold (1924) showed an 'organiser' region guides the embryo. Hox genes explain body layout. Sex is set by the Y chromosome gene SRY (1990). The 'organiser' experiment was done with newt embryos: a small piece of tissue grafted to another embryo made it grow a second body axis, which shows that cells instruct their neighbours. Von Baer's discovery of the egg in 1827 came when he found it in a dog's ovary. SRY, found by Peter Goodfellow and colleagues in 1990, switches on male development in the embryo; without it, the default is female development.
Watch out

Fix these The father's sperm decides the baby's sex (X or Y), not the mother. Ovulation does not always occur on day 14. The placenta is a filter, not a wall: some viruses and drugs cross. The mother always gives an X, so the sex of the baby depends on whether the sperm carries X or Y. The placenta carries oxygen, nutrients and some antibodies from mother to foetus, and wastes away from the foetus, via a thin membrane between two blood supplies that do not mix. Because of this, medicines and alcohol need care in pregnancy, and the Zika and rubella viruses can cross.
Birth and population in India

Dr Subhash Mukhopadhyay performed India's first IVF birth (Durga, Kolkata, 1978), only months after Louise Brown, but his work was not recognised during his lifetime. Dr T.C. Anand Kumar delivered India's first officially recorded IVF baby in 1986. India's total fertility rate dropped to about 2.0, under replacement level, per NFHS-5 (2019-21). Janani Suraksha Yojana (2005) promotes safe institutional births.
Key takeaways and questions

Gametes are haploid and made by meiosis. Cycle: FSH, oestrogen, LH surge, progesterone. Fertilisation, implantation, placenta, birth. IVF began in 1978. Think about it: Why does the placenta need to keep maternal and foetal blood apart? Why do pregnancy tests look for hCG? Key terms: the menstrual cycle lasts about 28 days: FSH grows a follicle, oestrogen thickens the uterine lining and triggers an LH surge, ovulation follows around mid-cycle, and progesterone from the corpus luteum keeps the lining until, if there is no pregnancy, it is shed. After implantation the embryo makes hCG, which keeps progesterone high, and this is what pregnancy tests detect in urine.
Microbes: Bacteria, Viruses and Fungi
The invisible majority

Microbes outnumber all other life. They cause diseases, but they also make curd, medicines, oxygen and soil fertility. You carry about as many bacterial cells as human ones. This lesson shows who they are. A single teaspoon of soil can hold billions of bacteria. They were Earth's first life, perhaps 3.5 billion years ago, and bacteria such as cyanobacteria created the oxygen in our air. In your gut they digest fibre and train your immune system. The microbial world includes bacteria, archaea, protists, fungi and viruses, which differ greatly in structure. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria with a homemade microscope around 1676, calling them 'animalcules'.
Three main groups

Bacteria: single prokaryotic cells with a cell wall. Viruses: genetic material in a protein coat, not cells. Fungi: eukaryotes with chitin walls, such as yeast, moulds and mushrooms. Archaea and protists add to the mix.
Bacteria

Shapes: rods (bacilli), spheres (cocci), spirals. They reproduce by dividing every 20 minutes in good conditions, swap genes through plasmids (conjugation) and may form tough spores. Gram staining (Hans Christian Gram, 1884) separates two wall types. Helpful: Lactobacillus (curd), Rhizobium (fixes nitrogen), gut flora. Harmful: cholera, TB, typhoid.
Viruses

A virus lands on a host cell, injects its genes, makes the cell build more viruses, and bursts out or buds off. Bacteriophages attack bacteria. Examples: influenza, HIV, SARS-CoV-2, rabies, dengue. Dmitri Ivanovsky (1892) and Beijerinck (1898) first showed tobacco mosaic disease is caused by something smaller than bacteria.
Fungi

Yeast (single cell) makes bread rise and brews alcohol. Moulds make penicillin: Alexander Fleming noticed Penicillium killing bacteria in 1928; Florey and Chain made it a drug in the 1940s (Nobel 1945). Fungi also cause athlete's foot, ringworm and, in weak patients, serious infections. Many form partnerships with roots (mycorrhiza) or algae (lichens).
Antibiotics and resistance

Antibiotics kill or stop bacteria, not viruses. If a few bacteria survive, they multiply and pass on resistance. Misuse speeds this. 'Superbugs' resist many drugs. Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould, Penicillium , killed bacteria around it, and Howard Florey and Ernst Chain made it into a drug in the 1940s. Different antibiotics attack different weak points: penicillin blocks cell wall building, which human cells do not have, so it harms bacteria but not us. Resistance arises by chance mutations and gene swapping. To slow it, finish the doctor's course, never use leftovers, and do not demand antibiotics for colds. Antimicrobial resistance is a serious problem in India.
Germ theory

Pasteur and Robert Koch proved germs cause disease in the 1860s-80s. Koch found the TB bacillus in 1882 and the cholera bacillus in 1883. Koch's postulates set the test. Joseph Lister (1867) used antiseptics. Electron microscopy first pictured viruses in the 1930s. Before germ theory, people blamed 'bad air' (miasma). Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation with his swan-neck flasks in 1859-61, and showed that heating (pasteurisation) kills microbes in milk. Koch's postulates: the germ must be found in every case, grown in pure culture, cause the disease when put in a healthy host, and be recovered again. Not every disease fits these rules, but they changed medicine. Lister's carbolic acid spray reduced surgical deaths sharply. John Snow traced cholera in London to a water pump in 1854.
Watch out

Fix these Most bacteria are harmless or helpful. Antibiotics do not treat colds or flu. Viruses are not killed by antibiotics because they have no cell machinery to target. Also, 'germs' include more than bacteria: viruses cause flu and measles, fungi cause ringworm and athlete's foot, and protists cause malaria. Washing hands with soap works by breaking the oily coat of many germs and lifting them off, and is among the most effective ways to prevent infection. Also, 'germs' include more than bacteria: viruses cause flu and measles, fungi cause ringworm and athlete's foot, and protists cause malaria. Washing hands with soap works by breaking the oily coat of many germs and lifting them off the skin, and is among the most effective ways to prevent infection. Sterilising and boiling water work by killing microbes with heat.
Microbes and India

Waldemar Haffkine, working in Mumbai in 1897, developed an early plague vaccine and a cholera vaccine. S.N. De at Kolkata (1959) showed that cholera toxin causes the disease. Indian curd, idli and dosa depend on microbes. Biogas and biofertilisers (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, blue-green algae) support farmers. India's national action plan on antimicrobial resistance began in 2017.
Key takeaways and questions

Bacteria are cells; viruses are not; fungi have chitin walls. Viruses hijack host cells. Antibiotics fight bacteria; misuse causes resistance. Fleming found penicillin in 1928. Think about it: Why is a course of antibiotics usually completed? Why is a virus harder to treat than bacteria?
Plants: Structure and Life
Quiet engineers

Plants feed us, clean our air, give timber, medicines and fibres, and hold soil. Knowing how they are built and how water moves in them explains farming, irrigation and why forests matter for climate. Plants have three main organs, roots, stems and leaves, and each is built from tissues for a particular job. Nearly all land plants rely on a vascular system, like a pipe network, for lifting water many metres. The tallest tree, a coast redwood, is about 115 metres, and water gets to its top without a pump. Plants also give us wood, cotton, rubber, and many medicines such as aspirin, whose origin is in willow bark, and quinine, from cinchona.
Plant groups

From simple to complex: bryophytes (mosses, no true vessels), pteridophytes (ferns, vessels but spores), gymnosperms (naked seeds: pine, cycas) and angiosperms (flowering plants, seeds in fruits). Angiosperms are the biggest group and split into monocots (one seed leaf, parallel veins) and dicots (two seed leaves, net veins).
Roots, stems, leaves

Roots: anchor, absorb water and minerals through root hairs. Stem: holds leaves up, carries fluids. Leaves: make food. Pores called stomata , opened by guard cells, let in CO2 and release water vapour and O2. Think of the plant as a factory with a supply pipe, a store and workshops. Root hairs are thin outgrowths that multiply the surface for absorption, and most land plants also work with fungi in mycorrhizae that help gather minerals. Leaves are broad and thin to catch light, with a waxy cuticle that limits water loss. A single large tree can lose hundreds of litres of water a day through its stomata, which is why they open and close in response to light and water.
Two transport tubes
Xylem carries water and minerals up from roots (dead tubes). Phloem carries sugar from leaves to where it is used (living tubes).
How water goes up a tall tree

No pump pushes it. Water evaporating from leaves ( transpiration ) pulls a continuous column, held together by cohesion between water molecules, like a drinking straw. This is the cohesion-tension idea (Dixon and Joly, 1894). Root pressure helps a little. Phloem uses pressure-flow (Ernst Munch, 1930).
Flowers and seeds

A flower is the reproductive organ. Pollen from the stamen lands on the stigma of the carpel and grows a tube to the ovule. Double fertilisation (found by Nawaschin and Guignard, 1898): one sperm makes the embryo, another forms the food tissue (endosperm). The ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit. Pollinators are bees, birds, bats and wind.
Plant hormones and responses

Auxin makes shoots bend to light (Darwin's 1880 coleoptile experiments; Went isolated auxin, 1928). Gibberellins make stems grow; cytokinins promote division; ethylene ripens fruit; abscisic acid closes stomata in drought. Day length controls flowering (photoperiodism). Darwin and his son Francis found in 1880 that a canary-grass shoot tip senses light and sends a signal that bends the stem below. Went proved the signal was a chemical, auxin. Auxin collects on the shaded side and makes cells there longer, so the shoot leans toward the light. Auxin-like chemicals are used as rooting powder and weed killers. Gibberellins were first found by Japanese scientists studying 'foolish seedling' disease in rice, which grew too tall.
Key experiments

Stephen Hales (1727) measured transpiration. Van Helmont's willow (1640s) hinted that plants gain mass from water. Barbara McClintock found jumping genes in maize (1940s, Nobel 1983). Hales measured how much water a sunflower lost through its leaves and showed that water moves up the plant. Van Helmont grew a willow tree for five years in a pot of weighed soil, and found that the soil lost only about 57 grams while the tree gained about 74 kg, so the tree did not get its mass from soil. McClintock's jumping genes, or transposons, were at first ignored but later found in nearly all life. Jagadish Chandra Bose, working in Kolkata around 1900, measured plant growth and responses with sensitive instruments.
Watch out

Fix these Roots do not 'suck' water; it is pulled up from above. Not all plants have flowers. Plants do not take food from soil, only water and minerals. Water rises in the xylem because water molecules stick to each other (cohesion) and to the walls of the narrow tubes, and evaporation from the leaves pulls the column up, a process known as the cohesion-tension theory, like drinking through a very long straw. Plants make their own food; from the soil they get water and minerals such as nitrate, phosphate and potassium, which are like vitamins and not food.
Plants and India

Birbal Sahni studied the fossil plant Pentoxylon and gymnosperms of Gondwana. J.C. Bose recorded plant movement. Ethnobotany, such as turmeric, neem, tulsi and the Ayurvedic plant stock, is part of daily life. Edavaluthu Kakkat Janaki Ammal (1897-1984), a plant cytogeneticist, worked on sugarcane and magnolias, and later led the Botanical Survey of India. India's Botanical Survey of India (1890) records about 55,000 plant species.
Key takeaways and questions

Plant groups: bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms. Xylem up (water), phloem down (sugar). Transpiration pull draws water up. Double fertilisation in angiosperms. Think about it: Why do plants wilt on hot afternoons? Why do farmers care about day length? Key terms: transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves, and it cools the plant and pulls water up. Phloem moves sugars from leaves to growing parts or stores by pressure flow. In a flower, pollen lands on the stigma and grows a tube to the ovule; one sperm fuses with the egg and another with two nuclei to form the food store ( endosperm ), a process found by Nawaschin in 1898, called double fertilisation.
Animals: A Tour of the Kingdoms
A family of over a million

About 1.3 to 1.5 million animal species have been named, and most are insects. Knowing the main groups, and how each is built, shows how body plans evolved and why habitats matter for conservation. Insects alone account for over half of all named species, and beetles are the most numerous group, a remark attributed to the biologist J.B.S. Haldane, who said that the Creator had 'an inordinate fondness for beetles'. India is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, with about 100,000 recorded animal species, including tigers, Asian elephants and the one-horned rhinoceros. Animals in turn pollinate plants, recycle matter and control pests.
What makes an animal

Animals are multicellular eukaryotes that eat other organisms, have no cell walls, and most can move at some stage. They are grouped by body plan: symmetry, body layers, a body cavity, segmentation and a backbone. The first animals appeared in the sea more than 600 million years ago. Most animals show bilateral symmetry , with left and right halves, which suits moving in one direction and goes along with a head end (cephalisation). Jellyfish and sea anemones have radial symmetry , like a wheel, and sponges have none. Animals also differ in whether the embryo has two or three tissue layers and whether there is a fluid-filled body cavity, the coelom. Animals take in food by eating, unlike plants, which make theirs.
Invertebrates: no backbone

Porifera (sponges): pores, no true tissues. Cnidaria: jellyfish, coral, stinging cells. Platyhelminthes: flatworms, tapeworm. Nematoda: roundworms. Annelida: segmented worms like earthworms. Mollusca: snails, octopus, soft body. Arthropoda: insects, spiders, crabs. Jointed legs and a chitin shell. The largest phylum. Echinodermata: starfish, spiny skin. Think of each phylum as a different blueprint. Sponges filter water through pores, much as a sieve does. Cnidarians have two tissue layers and tentacles with stinging cells (cnidocytes). Flatworms are flat, with no body cavity, so every cell is near the surface. Roundworms have a gut with two openings, while earthworms are divided into repeated segments, and Indian earthworms improve soil. Molluscs have a muscular foot and often a shell; octopus and squid are clever molluscs. Arthropods shed their hard coat as they grow (moulting), and echinoderms move by water-filled tube feet.
Vertebrates: with a backbone
All belong to phylum Chordata. Five classes:
Key features of chordates

At some stage, all chordates have a notochord, a hollow nerve cord above it, and gill slits. In vertebrates the notochord becomes the backbone. Warm-blooded animals (birds, mammals) keep a steady body temperature using energy; cold-blooded ones rely on the environment. The chordate groups are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Fish breathe with gills and have fins; amphibians, such as frogs, live partly on land and partly in water and have moist skin; reptiles have dry scaly skin and lay shelled eggs; birds have feathers and hollow bones; and mammals have hair and feed milk to their young. The terms 'warm-blooded' and 'cold-blooded' are better written as endotherm and ectotherm , and a snake basking in the sun is using its surroundings to warm up.
Insects: the champions

Insects have three body parts, six legs and often wings. Many go through metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult in butterflies). Bees, ants and termites live in complex societies. Karl von Frisch decoded the honeybee waggle dance (Nobel 1973). A butterfly's change is called complete metamorphosis, in which the caterpillar eats and grows, then the pupa rebuilds the body, and the adult flies away to mate. A grasshopper has incomplete metamorphosis, with young nymphs that look like small adults. Insects breathe through tiny tubes called tracheae, not lungs, and the hard chitin skeleton must be shed to grow. Insects pollinate about three-quarters of food crops, and honeybees are crucial. In the waggle dance, the angle of the dance gives the direction relative to the Sun, and its length gives the distance.
Mammal groups

Egg-laying mammals (monotremes: platypus), pouched mammals (marsupials: kangaroo) and placental mammals (most). Whales and bats show how a mammal can return to water or learn to fly. Monotremes, such as the platypus and echidna, lay eggs yet feed their young with milk. Marsupials give birth to tiny young that finish growing in a pouch, and most live in Australia and the Americas. Placental mammals nourish the foetus through a placenta, and include rodents, bats, whales, elephants and primates. Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, and whales' ancestors walked on land, a story shown by fossils from Pakistan and India.
Classifying animals

Linnaeus (1758) set the base. Cuvier grouped animals by body plan (1812). Today DNA sequences revise trees: for example, birds are living dinosaurs, and whales are close kin to hippos. Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae gave every species a two-part Latin name and nested groups: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. A useful memory aid is that closer relatives share more levels. Cuvier, who also helped found the study of extinction, showed that fossil animals were different from living ones. DNA evidence has shown that hippos are the closest living relatives of whales, and that birds belong inside the dinosaur group, since small feathered theropods gave rise to them.
Watch out

Fix these Spiders are not insects (eight legs, two body parts). Whales and bats are mammals, not fish or birds. A jellyfish or starfish is not a fish. Also, a bat is not a bird: it has fur, gives birth to live young and feeds them milk, and its wing is a skin stretched over elongated finger bones. Whales breathe air through lungs and have to surface. Dolphins and sharks look alike through convergent evolution , where similar needs (fast swimming) shape different lineages into similar forms. Remember too that 'worm' is not a group: flatworms, roundworms and earthworms belong to three different phyla.
India's wildlife

India shelters tiger, Asian elephant, Asiatic lion (only in Gir, Gujarat), one-horned rhinoceros and the gharial. Project Tiger began in 1973 and India now has more than 3,000 tigers by the 2022 count (3,682 estimated). Project Cheetah (2022) reintroduced cheetahs from Namibia and South Africa. Salim Ali (1896-1987), the Birdman of India, wrote the Book of Indian Birds (1941). The Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 protects species.
Key takeaways and questions

Animals are grouped by body plan. Arthropods are the largest phylum. Five vertebrate classes: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals. Many species exist only in India's special habitats. Think about it: Why can amphibians not live far from water? Why is warm-bloodedness both costly and useful?
Ecology and Ecosystems
Everything is connected

Remove tigers, and deer may boom; remove bees, and crops fall. Ecology studies how living things relate to each other and to their surroundings. It underpins climate policy, farming and conservation. Ecologists often study food webs. When wolves were removed from Yellowstone in the 1920s, elk grew in number and grazed willow along rivers heavily. Likewise, in India, the decline of vultures in the 1990s after the veterinary drug diclofenac poisoned them led to more feral dogs and a risk of rabies, a case showing how one species' loss ripples. Ecology therefore connects organisms to water, soil, climate and people.
Levels of ecology

Organism, population (one species in one place), community (all species), ecosystem (community plus non-living environment: water, soil, light) and biosphere. The word 'ecology' was coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866; 'ecosystem' by Arthur Tansley in 1935. Take a pond as an example: one fish is an organism, all the fish of one species make a population, fish, plants, insects and microbes together are a community, and add the water, mud, sunlight and dissolved oxygen to get an ecosystem. The biosphere is the thin layer of Earth where life exists, from the deep sea to about the clouds. Within each ecosystem, a habitat is the place an organism lives, and its niche is its role.
Food chains and energy flow

Energy enters as sunlight and moves up through producers (plants), herbivores , carnivores and decomposers . Only about 10 percent of energy passes to the next level (Lindeman, 1942), the rest is lost as heat. That is why food chains are short and there are fewer tigers than deer.
Cycles of matter

Matter recycles; energy does not. Carbon cycle: CO2 taken in by photosynthesis, returned by respiration and burning. Nitrogen cycle: bacteria fix N2 into usable forms; others return it to air. Water cycle: evaporation, rain, runoff. Extra CO2 from fossil fuels is warming Earth. Think of it as a one-way street for energy and a roundabout for matter. In the nitrogen cycle, bacteria in the root nodules of pulses such as peas and gram fix nitrogen from air, which is why farmers rotate pulses with cereals. Other bacteria turn waste into ammonia and nitrates, and denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the air. Fritz Haber's ammonia process (1909) now supplies fertiliser, though runoff can cause algal blooms in lakes. Charles Keeling's curve shows CO2 above 420 ppm.
Populations and interactions

Populations grow fast at first, then level off at the carrying capacity . Species interact by competition, predation, parasitism, mutualism (bees and flowers) and commensalism. Keystone species, like tigers, wolves and sea otters, have an outsized effect. A growth curve is S-shaped: slow start, rapid rise as resources are abundant, and then levelling off as food, space or disease limit the population. Mutualism helps both sides: bees get nectar and flowers get pollinated. Parasitism helps one at the other's cost, as with ticks. A keystone species has an effect far beyond its numbers: sea otters keep sea urchins in check, which protects kelp forests, as Robert Paine's starfish removal experiments of the 1960s also showed. Tigers help keep the whole forest healthy by controlling herbivore numbers.
Succession and biomes

Bare rock turns to forest through ecological succession : lichens, mosses, grasses, shrubs, trees. Major biomes are tundra, taiga, temperate forest, grassland, desert, tropical rainforest and aquatic zones. Climate sets the biome. On bare rock, hardy pioneer species such as lichens begin, making thin soil as they die and decay, which lets mosses and grasses take hold, and later shrubs and trees. The final stable community is the climax . India shows many biomes: the Thar desert, the Himalayan alpine zone, tropical rainforest in the Western Ghats and Northeast, mangroves in the Sundarbans and grasslands in the Terai. Rainfall and temperature, more than anything else, decide which biome forms in a place.
Biodiversity and threats

Threats: habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, over-harvest and climate change (summed up as HIPPO). Conservation is by protected areas (in situ: national parks, reserves) or off-site (ex situ: zoos, seed banks). Edward O. Wilson popularised the term biodiversity. Biodiversity means variety at three levels: genes, species and ecosystems. India holds about 8 percent of the world's species on 2.4 percent of its land area, and four global hotspots (the Himalaya, Western Ghats, Indo-Burma and Sundaland). Project Tiger, begun in 1973, and the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 are examples of in situ conservation. Ex situ options include botanical gardens, seed banks and captive breeding, such as for the Asiatic lion's second home. Healthy ecosystems also provide services like clean water and pollination.
Classic studies

Tansley (1935) and Lindeman (1942) quantified energy flow. Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) showed pesticide DDT harmed birds. Wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995 and rivers and plants changed (trophic cascade). Keeling's curve has shown CO2 rising since 1958. Raymond Lindeman's work on a lake showed that only about 10 percent of energy passes from one level to the next, which is why food chains are short and why there are few top predators. Rachel Carson's book showed that DDT builds up through the food chain ( biomagnification ) and thins bird eggshells, and helped lead to the ban on DDT use in farming in the US in 1972. Reintroducing wolves at Yellowstone is a well-known but still debated example of a trophic cascade.
Watch out

Fix these Energy does not cycle; matter does. The top predator is not the 'most important'; every link matters. Climate and weather are different: climate is the long-term pattern. Also, ecosystems can recover, but not always to what they were: some changes, such as the loss of a coral reef, are hard to reverse. 'Natural' does not mean unchanging, either. Weather is what happens today; climate is the average over at least thirty years, so one cold day does not disprove warming. Also, a food web is not a ladder: an animal such as a bear or a human eats at several levels, so removing one species can have effects that are hard to predict. Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria are just as vital, since they return nutrients to the soil.
Conservation in India

India has about 100 national parks and over 500 wildlife sanctuaries. Chipko (1973) and the Bishnoi tradition show community conservation. The Biological Diversity Act (2002) and Wildlife (Protection) Act (1972) give legal protection. Silent Valley (Kerala) was saved from a dam in the 1980s. Sundarbans is the world's largest mangrove delta. Madhav Gadgil's Western Ghats work shaped debates. India pledged net zero by 2070 at COP26 (2021).
Key takeaways and questions

Energy flows one way; matter cycles. About 10 percent passes up each level. Biodiversity loss is driven mostly by habitat change. Conservation: in situ and ex situ. Think about it: Why is a vegetarian diet more energy-efficient? Why do keystone species matter more than their numbers suggest?
Disease, Pandemics and Public Health
From plague to COVID

Infectious disease has shaped history: the Black Death, smallpox, the 1918 flu and COVID-19. Public health, meaning clean water, vaccines and surveillance, has saved more lives than most drugs. This lesson ties microbes, immunity and society together. The Black Death of the 1300s killed perhaps a third of Europe, and the 1918 influenza killed an estimated 50 million people worldwide, many in India. Disease patterns follow cities, trade and travel. Public health works by prevention: sanitation, clean water, vaccination, nutrition and tracking cases. When John Snow removed the handle of a Broad Street pump in London in 1854, cholera cases dropped, a founding example of epidemiology .
Types of disease

Infectious: caused by germs and can spread (cholera, TB, malaria). Non-communicable: not spread, such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer. Deficiency and genetic diseases form other groups. Disease spreads through air, water, food, vectors (mosquitoes), blood or contact. Think of an endemic disease as always present in a region (malaria in some districts), an epidemic as a sudden rise above normal, and a pandemic as one that spreads across continents. Spread routes matter for control: airborne diseases need masks and ventilation, waterborne diseases need clean water and sanitation, and vector-borne diseases need mosquito control. A carrier can pass on an infection without showing symptoms, as Typhoid Mary did in the early 1900s. Non-communicable diseases now cause most deaths in India.
Epidemic, endemic, pandemic
Endemic: steady in a region (malaria in some districts). Epidemic: sudden rise in a place. Pandemic: spread across the world (1918 flu, COVID-19, declared March 2020).
The R number and control

R0 is how many people one case infects on average. Above 1, the outbreak grows; below 1, it fades. Control tools: vaccination, isolation, masks, clean water, vector control, contact tracing. John Snow (1854) traced cholera in London to the Broad Street pump, the start of epidemiology.
Major infections

Malaria: Plasmodium, spread by female Anopheles. Ronald Ross showed this in 1897 in India (Secunderabad). TB: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, airborne. HIV/AIDS: virus attacks helper T cells. Dengue, chikungunya: Aedes mosquitoes. Cholera, typhoid: contaminated water. Malaria is caused by a single-celled parasite, which infects the liver and then red blood cells, causing cycles of fever. Ronald Ross, working at the Presidency General Hospital in Secunderabad, found the parasite in a mosquito's stomach in 1897 and won the 1902 Nobel Prize. TB is treated with a long course of several antibiotics, and stopping early encourages drug-resistant strains. Dengue spreads in cities because Aedes breeds in clean, stored water such as in coolers and old tyres, so emptying containers weekly helps.
Zoonoses and new outbreaks

Many new diseases jump from animals: Ebola, SARS, MERS, COVID-19, Nipah, avian flu. Habitat loss and wildlife trade raise the chance. The 'One Health' idea links human, animal and environmental health. A zoonosis is a disease passing from animals to humans, and about three-fifths of known human infections originate in animals. Nipah virus, carried by fruit bats, caused outbreaks in Kerala in 2018 and later. Rabies, mostly from dog bites, kills thousands in India each year, but can be prevented by vaccination of dogs and prompt post-bite treatment. Because people, animals and environment are linked, One Health teams include doctors, vets and ecologists who share data and plans.
Eradication stories

Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, the first human disease wiped out. Polio is nearly gone. Rinderpest in cattle was eradicated in 2011. Wuchereria and Guinea worm are close to elimination. mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 were developed within a year (Karikó and Weissman, Nobel 2023).
Watch out

Fix these Pandemic means wide spread, not severity. Not all disease is caused by germs. Vaccines and hygiene, not just drugs, are the main tools. Also, how bad an outbreak is depends on three things: how easily it spreads, how severe it is and how well people are protected. Public health measures such as hand washing, clean water, vaccination and contact tracing work together, and the eradication of smallpox in 1980 and the near-elimination of polio (India was declared polio-free in 2014) show the power of this approach. Also, handwashing and clean water are public health tools too.
India's health programmes

The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme tackles malaria and dengue. The TB programme (now NTEP) offers free DOTS treatment. India eliminated Guinea worm (2000) and trachoma as a public health problem (2024), and was declared maternal and neonatal tetanus free in 2015. Ayushman Bharat (2018) provides health insurance, and the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (2004) tracks outbreaks. ICMR's National Institute of Virology in Pune isolated the first SARS-CoV-2 strain in India in 2020. Malaria deaths fell sharply since 2000.
Key takeaways and questions

Infectious versus non-communicable diseases. Endemic, epidemic, pandemic. R below 1 ends an outbreak. Zoonoses are a rising threat; One Health is the answer. Think about it: Why did smallpox eradication succeed but measles has not yet? How would you decide when to close schools in an outbreak?
